text:
5 Time Series Forecasting Process

Collect data and split into training and test sets
Create & Fit Multiple Models
Add fitted models to a Model Table
Calibrate the models to a testing set.
Perform Testing Set Forecast & Accuracy Evaluation
Refit the models to Full Dataset & Forecast Forward


5.1 Step 1: Data Import and Sampling
In the code chunk below, read_rds() from the readr package is used to load the saved .rds file into the R environment. The variables id, store_nbr, and family are then converted into factors instead of numeric values. Next, the data is grouped by family and date, and the total sales for each product family on each date are calculated. After the summarisation step, the data is ungrouped.
During execution, R prints the message “summarise() has grouped output by ‘family’”. This occurs because when summarise() is applied to a dataset grouped by multiple variables, dplyr removes only the last grouping variable (in this case date) and keeps the remaining grouping variable (family). Therefore, the resulting dataset is still grouped by family, and R displays this message to inform the user that grouping has not been completely removed.
We then apply ungroup() to remove the remaining grouping structure. This is necessary because subsequent operations, such as mutations, lags, or time series modelling, may otherwise be calculated separately within each family group, which can lead to unintended behaviour or incorrect results. Ungrouping ensures the dataset returns to a standard tibble format so later analysis and forecasting procedures work as expected.

grocery <- read_rds(
  "data/store_sales/grocery.rds") %>%
  mutate(across(c(1, 3, 4), as.factor)) %>%
  group_by(family, date) %>%
  summarise(sum_sales = sum(sales)) %>%
  ungroup()

We can also import the rest of the data sets provided at Kaggle by using the code chunk below.

holidays_events <- read_csv(
  "data/store_sales/holidays_events.csv")
oil <- read_csv(
  "data/store_sales/oil.csv")
stores <- read_csv(
  "data/store_sales/stores.csv")
transactions <- read_csv(
  "data/store_sales/transactions.csv")

    date,
    sum_sales,

grocery tibble data frame consists of 1684 days of daily sales data starts from 1st January 2013 to 15 August 2018. We will split the data set into training and hold-out data sets by using initial_time_split() of rsample package, a member of the tidymodels family.

splits <- grocery %>%
  initial_time_split(prop = 0.955)
training <- training(splits)
holdout <- testing(splits)


prop: the proportion of traing data for modeling/analysis. Here we have about 95.5% 1608 days for training and 76 days for testing.
splits is an rsplit object that stores row indices.
training() and testing() from rsample are used to retrieve the spliting results from the splits object.

5.2 Step 2: Create & Fit Multiple Models
In this step, we will build and fit four models using the code chunks below:
Model 1: Exponential Smoothing (Modeltime)
An Error-Trend-Season (ETS) model by using exp_smoothing().

model_fit_ets <- exp_smoothing() %>%
  set_engine(engine = "ets") %>%
  fit(sum_sales ~ `date`,
      data = training)

Sales follow a weekly repeating pattern.
Model 2: Auto ARIMA (Modeltime)
An auto ARIMA model by using arima_reg().
arima_reg() is a way to generate a specification of an ARIMA model before fitting and allows the model to be created using different packages.

model_fit_arima <- arima_reg() %>%
  set_engine(engine = "auto_arima") %>%
  fit(sum_sales ~ `date`,
      data = training)

Model 3: Boosted Auto ARIMA (Modeltime)
An Boosted auto ARIMA model by using arima_boost().
arima_boost() is a hybrid model that uses boosting to improve modeling errors (residuals) on Exogenous Regressors .It first uses ARIMA to capture the main time series structure (trend and seasonality), and then applies gradient boosting (XGBoost) to model the remaining errors that ARIMA cannot explain.
The main algorithms are:

Auto ARIMA + XGBoost Errors (engine = auto_arima_xgboost, default)
ARIMA + XGBoost Errors (engine = arima_xgboost)

The first algorithm performs automatic ARIMA parameter selection, which is convenient but can be slower because the model searches through many possible combinations. The second algorithm is more suitable when the time series behaviour is already understood, since the ARIMA structure can be specified directly (in p,d,q, P, D, Q).
We can also apply time series cross validation to compare the forecasting performance of the two models and determine which produces more accurate predictions.

library(tune)

start_time <- Sys.time()
cat("Starting modeling at:", format(Sys.time(), "%H:%M:%S"), "\n")

model_fit_arima_boosted <- arima_boost(
  min_n = 2,
  learn_rate = 0.015
) %>%
  set_engine(
    engine = "auto_arima_xgboost",
    trace = TRUE
  ) %>%
  fit(sum_sales ~ date,
      data = training)

cat("Model completed at:", format(end_time, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), 
    "\nDuration:", round(as.numeric(duration, units = "mins"), 2), "minutes\n")

Model completed at: 2026-03-02 00:27:52 
Duration: 0.63 minutes



min_n = 2 sets the minimum number of observations required in each boosting tree node.
learn_rate = 0.015 controls how aggressively the boosting model learns. A small value makes learning slower but usually improves stability and reduces overfitting.

Model 4: prophet (Modeltime)
A prophet model using prophet_reg().
Prophet is a time series forecasting algorithm designed for business data such as: retail sales, web traffic, demand forecasting.
It works especially well when data has: • trend changes • strong seasonality • holidays and events • missing values or outliers
Unlike ARIMA, Prophet is not purely statistical and is a decomposable additive regression model.

model_fit_prophet <- prophet_reg() %>%
  set_engine(engine = "prophet") %>%
  fit(sum_sales ~ `date`, 
      data = training)

Prophet can forecast CPI, but it should be treated as a complementary model, not a replacement. CPI often favours ARIMA, while Prophet is valuable when inflation trends change or structural breaks occur.
prophet_boost() might be good fit for CPI but suitable for grocery sales, similar to arima boost, it also create a hybrid model.
Model 5: Linear Regression (Parsnip)
We can model time series linear regression (TSLM) using the linear_reg() algorithm from parsnip.

start_time <- Sys.time()
cat("Starting modeling at:", format(Sys.time(), "%H:%M:%S"), "\n")

Starting modeling at: 00:27:53 

model_fit_lm <- linear_reg() %>%
    set_engine("lm") %>%
    fit(sum_sales ~ as.numeric(date) + 
            factor(month(date, label = TRUE), ordered = FALSE) + # Add month
            factor(wday(date, label = TRUE), ordered = FALSE),  # Add day of week
        data = training(splits))

end_time <- Sys.time()
duration <- end_time - start_time
cat("Model completed at:", format(end_time, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), 
    "\nDuration:", round(as.numeric(duration, units = "mins"), 2), "minutes\n")

Model completed at: 2026-03-02 00:27:53 
Duration: 0 minutes



5.3 Model 6: MARS (Workflow)
We can model a Multivariate Adaptive Regression Spline model using mars().

library(earth)

model_spec_mars <- mars(mode = "regression") %>%
    set_engine("earth")

# Recipe with both month AND day-of-week for daily grocery data
recipe_spec_mars <- recipe(sum_sales ~ date, data = training(splits)) %>%
    # Date features
    step_date(date, features = c("month", "dow"), ordinal = FALSE) %>%
    step_mutate(
        date_num = as.numeric(date),
        # Optional: add day of month for month-end effects
        day_of_month = day(date)
    ) %>%
    step_normalize(date_num) %>%
    # Create dummy variables from factors
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
    step_rm(date)

# Fit the workflow
wflw_fit_mars <- workflow() %>%
    add_recipe(recipe_spec_mars) %>%
    add_model(model_spec_mars) %>%
    fit(training(splits))


5.4 Step 3: Add Fitted Models to a Model Table
Next, modeltime_table() of modeltime package is used to add each of the models to a Modeltime Table.

models_tbl <- modeltime_table(
    model_fit_ets,
    model_fit_arima,
    model_fit_arima_boosted,
    model_fit_prophet,
    model_fit_lm,
    wflw_fit_mars
)

5.5 Step 4: Calibrate the Model to a Testing Set
modeltime_calibrate() adds a new column, .calibration_data, with the test predictions and residuals inside from the hold-out data.

calibration_tbl <- models_tbl %>%
    modeltime_calibrate(new_data = testing(splits))

5.6 Step 5: Model Accuracy Assessment
5A: Visualising the Forecast Test
plot_modeltime_forecast() from timetk is used.

p <- calibration_tbl %>%
    modeltime_forecast(
        new_data = testing(splits),
        actual_data = grocery
    ) %>%
    plot_modeltime_forecast(
        .legend_max_width = 25,
        .interactive = FALSE
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(as.Date("2017-04-01"), as.Date("2017-08-01"))) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2017-06-01"), linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5)  # mark forecast start

5B: Accuracy Metrics
We can use modeltime_accuracy() to calculate common accuracy metrics and table_modeltime_accuracy() to display the output. The table becomes similar to a dt table when interactive is enabled.
The winner model is ARIMA(1,0,3)(2,1,2)[7], as it achieves the lowest RMSE value (29,829) among all models. This indicates that its forecasts are closest to the actual observed sales overall. The RMSE also suggests that the model’s daily predictions typically deviate from the true grocery sales by approximately 29.8 thousand units on average.

2 Getting Started

2.1 Installing and Loading the Required Libraries
There are 4 packages that will be used in this exercise.


Package
Description



tidyverse
A collection of R packages for data importing, cleaning, transformation, and visualisation (e.g., readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2).


lubridate
A Tidyverse package that handles date-time objects

Provides ‘ggplot2’ themes and scales that replicate some of the famous looks.

3 Step 1: Data Import
For this hands-on exercise, the Average Retail Prices of Selected Consumer Items file will be used. It contains 7,452 rows of time series records of average retail prices for selected consumer items.

3.1 Importing the Data
We use read_csv() from the readr package to import the dataset AVERP.csv into the R environment as a tibble named df. We then preview the dataset using kable().

averp <- read_csv("data/AVERP.csv")

The dataset contains three columns: two categorical variables, Date and Consumer Items, and one numeric column Values. Since we want to perform time series plotting, it is essential to convert the Date to proper date data type. Here we use dmy() from lubridate pacakge to convert the column into date format.

averp <- averp %>%
  mutate(`Date` = dmy(`Date`))

3.2 Step 2. Plotting the horizon graph
Horizon plots compare each consumer item to its own history/pattern of average retail prices while line plots with same scales compare the average prices to each other. The code below creates a horizon plot by using geom_horizon() from ggHoriPlot package. “%b%y” in date_labels controls the format of date that displays under the x-axis. “3-month” of date_breaksset the labels only shows every 3 months.

averp %>%
  filter(Date >= "2018-01-01") %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_horizon(aes(x = Date, y = Values),
               origin = "midpoint",
               horizonscale = 6) +
facet_grid(`Consumer Items`~.) +
  theme_few() +
  scale_fill_hcl(palette = 'RdBu') +
  theme(panel.spacing.y = unit(0, "lines"),
        strip.text.y = element_text(
          size = 5, angle = 0, hjust = 0
        ),
        legend.position = 'none',
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) +
  scale_x_date(expand = c(0,0), date_breaks = "3 month", date_labels = "%b%y") +
  ggtitle('Average Retail Prices of Selected Consumer Items(Jan 2018 to Dec 2022)')

title: 08-3 Analytical Mapping
text:
In this in class exercise, we gain practical experience using appropriate R techniques to create analytical maps.

By the end of this exercise, we learn how to apply functions from the tmap and tidyverse packages to complete the following tasks:

Import geospatial datasets stored in RDS format into the R environment.
Create cartographic quality choropleth maps using suitable functions from the tmap package.
Produce rate map to visualise values relative to a population or area.
Generate percentile map to compare the relative distribution of values across regions.
Construct boxmap to highlight spatial outliers and variations in the dataset.

title: 08-3 Analytical Mapping
text:
3 Basic Choropleth Mapping
The code chunk below generates a basic map of the study area, Nigeria.

tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "grey80") +
  tm_title("Map of LGAs in Nigeria")







The code below creates a choropleth map for total water points by using functions from tmap package and set classification style as “equal”.

tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "total_wp",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal",
      n = 10,
      values = "brewer.blues"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Total Water Points",
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")
    ),
    col = "grey", 
    lwd = 0.1 
  ) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Total Water Points by LGAs")








3.1 Visualising Distribution of Non-functional Water Points
The code below creates two maps for function and non-function water points in the study area.

p1 <- tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "wp_functional",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal",
      n = 10,
      values = "brewer.blues"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Functional Water Points",
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")
    ),
    col = "grey", 
    lwd = 0.1 
  ) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Functional Water Points by LGAs")
p1








p2 <- tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "wp_nonfunctional",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal",
      n = 10,
      values = "brewer.reds"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Non-functional Water Points",
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")
    ),
    col = "grey", 
    lwd = 0.1 
  ) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Non-functional Water Points by LGAs")
p2







Next we arrange them side by side.

tmap_arrange(p1,p2, nrow = 1)







The maps show that functional water points are generally concentrated in the northern part of the study area, whereas non functional water points appear more frequently in the central regions. However, the scales of the two maps differ significantly. Functional water points reach a maximum value of 752, while non functional water points only total 278. As a result, comparisons based on absolute values may lead to misleading interpretations.

title: 08-3 Analytical Mapping
text:
4 Choropleth Map for Rates
Previous readings have emphasised the importance of mapping rates instead of raw counts. This is because water points are unevenly distributed across space. Without adjusting for the number of water points in each location, the map would simply reflect the overall concentration of water points, rather than revealing meaningful spatial patterns related to the phenomenon being studied.

4.1 Deriving Proportion of Functional Water Points and Non-Functional Water Points
The code below uses the mutate() function from the dplyr package to create two new variables representing the percentage of functional and non functional water points relative to the total number of water points.

NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  mutate(pct_functional = wp_functional/total_wp) %>%
    mutate(pct_nonfunctional = wp_nonfunctional/total_wp)

title: 08-3 Analytical Mapping
text:
5 Extreme Value Maps
Extreme value maps are a variation of traditional choropleth maps in which the classification scheme is designed to highlight extreme values at both the lower and upper ends of the scale. The main goal is to identify potential outliers in the data. These maps were developed in the context of spatial exploratory data analysis (EDA), which extends common non spatial EDA techniques by incorporating spatial information (Anselin, 1994).

5.1 Percentile Map
A percentile map is a special type of quantile map that uses six specific categories: 0–1%, 1–10%, 10–50%, 50–90%, 90–99%, and 99–100%. The corresponding breakpoints can be calculated using the base R quantile() function, by specifying a vector of cumulative probabilities such as c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1). It is important to include both the starting point (0) and the ending point (1) to ensure that the full range of values is represented.

5.1.1 Data Preparation
Step 1: Exclude records with NA by using the code chunk below.

NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  drop_na()


sum(is.na(NGA_wp))

[1] 0


Step 2: Creating customised classification and extracting values

percent <- c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1)
var <- NGA_wp["pct_functional"] %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL)
quantile(var[,1], percent)

       0%        1%       10%       50%       90%       99%      100% 
0.0000000 0.0000000 0.2169811 0.4791667 0.8611111 1.0000000 1.0000000 








Important



When variables are extracted from an sf data frame, the geometry column is included automatically. While this is useful for spatial analysis, many base R functions cannot handle geometry. For example, quantile() will produce an error. Therefore, st_set_geometry(NULL) is used to remove the geometry column.



5.1.2 Why writing functions?
Writing a function has several advantages compared to copy and paste. First, a function can be given a clear name that improves code readability. Second, when requirements change, the code only needs to be updated in one place. Third, it reduces the risk of mistakes that may occur when copying and modifying code repeatedly.
Source: Chapter 19, Functions, R for Data Science.

5.1.3 Creating the get.var function
First, we create an R function to extract a variable (e.g., wp_nonfunctional) as a vector from an sf data frame.
Arguments:

vname: the variable name (as a character string, in quotes)
df: the name of the sf data frame

Returns:
-v: a vector containing the values (without a column name).

get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>%
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v<- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}


5.1.4 A percentile mapping function
Next, we will write a percentile mapping function by using the code chunk below.

percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle=NA, mtitle="Percentile Map",
                       palette = "brewer.blues"){
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  var <- as.vector(unlist(var))
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent, na.rm = TRUE)
  bperc <- bperc + seq_along(bperc) * 1e-10
  
  tm_shape(df) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = vnam,
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        breaks = bperc,
        values = palette
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = legtitle,
        labels = c("<1%", "1%-10%", "10%-50%", "50%-90%", "90%-99%", ">99%")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders() +
     tm_title(mtitle) +  
    tm_layout(title.position = c("right", "top"))
}


5.1.5 Test drive the percentile mapping function

percentmap("total_wp", NGA_wp)








p5 <- percentmap("wp_functional", NGA_wp,
                 legtitle = "Functional",
                 mtitle = "Percentile Map: Functional Water Points",
                 palette = "brewer.blues")

p6 <- percentmap("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp,
                 legtitle = "Non-functional",
                 mtitle = "Percentile Map: Non-functional Water Points",
                 palette = "brewer.reds")  

tmap_arrange(p5, p6, nrow = 1)








5.2 Box Map
A box map is an enhanced version of a quartile map that includes additional categories to highlight lower and upper outliers. When lower outliers exist, the first break is set at the minimum value and the second break at the lower fence. If there are no lower outliers, the first break begins at the lower fence followed by the minimum value, since no observations fall between these two values.

ggplot(data = NGA_wp,
       aes(x = "",
           y = wp_nonfunctional)) +
  geom_boxplot()








5.2.1 Creating the boxbreaks Function
The code chunk below defines an R function that generates breakpoints for constructing a box map.
Arguments:


v:a vector containing the observations

-mult: multiplier for the IQR (default value is 1.5)
Returns:
-bb: a vector of seven breakpoints based on the quartiles and fences.

boxbreaks <- function(v,mult=1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialize break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode="numeric",length=7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) { # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}


5.2.2 Creating the get.var function
Here we should create a same R function to extract a variable as a vector.
Arguments:

vname: the variable name (as a character string, in quotes)
df: the name of the sf data frame

Returns:
-v: a vector containing the values (without a column name).

get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>%
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v<- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}


5.2.3 Test drive the newly created function

var <- get.var("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp) 
boxbreaks(var)

[1] -56.5   0.0  14.0  34.0  61.0 131.5 278.0



5.2.4 Boxmap function

boxmap <- function(vnam, df, 
                   legtitle=NA,
                   mtitle="Box Map",
                   mult=1.5,
                   palette = "brewer.blues"){
  var <- get.var(vnam,df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  
  tm_shape(df) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = vnam,
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
             breaks=bb,
             values=palette
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = legtitle,
        labels = c("lower outlier", 
                     "< 25%", 
                     "25% - 50%", 
                     "50% - 75%",
                     "> 75%", 
                     "upper outlier")))+
  tm_borders() +
   tm_title(mtitle) +  
    tm_layout(title.position = c("right", "top"))
}


p7 <- boxmap("wp_functional", NGA_wp)
p8 <- boxmap("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp, palette = "brewer.reds")
tmap_arrange(p7, p8, nrow = 1)







The box maps illustrate the enhanced spatial distribution of functional and non functional water points across Nigeria. Functional water points appear to be more concentrated in the northern regions, while non functional water points show higher concentrations in several central and southern areas. The box map classification helps identify outlier regions with unusually high or low values,that helps us to form a clearer understanding of spatial variation.

title: 08-1 Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
A Choropleth map is a thematic map that represents statistical data by shading predefined geographic areas such as countries, provinces, states, counties, or consus units with varying colours or patterns. The intensity or shade reflects the magnitude of variable within each spatial unit. For instance the researcher might use a choropleth map to illustrate how the proportion of elderly residents varies across singapore’s must plan 2014 subsume boundaries.
In this chapter we will learn how to create clear accurate and meaningful Chrome plus map using the team map package in R with an emphasis on producing maps that communicate data effectively and responsibly.

title: 08-1 Choropleth Mapping with R
section: 4 Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap
text:
4 Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap

Choropleth mapping shows data by colouring areas such as countries, states, or census zones, using shades or patterns to represent values.

4.1 Plotting a choropleth map quickly by using qtm()

qtm() stands for Quick Thematic Map to plot quick, simple maps.

tmap_mode("plot")         #plot: static; view: interactive
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2020,
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")   #attribute/column








4.2 Creating Cchoropleth Map by Using tmap’s Elements
tmap elements: for detailed, highly customisable maps (with multiple Cartographic furniture)

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(  #it depends nature of the map, choose appropriate one from tm_scale family, tm_scale_rgb() etc.
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by Planning Subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone Boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Popluation Data from Department of Statistics DOS",
             position = c("left","bottom"),
             just = c("left","bottom"),
             outside = TRUE)








4.2.1 Drawing a Base map Using tm_shape()

The code uses tm_shape() to supply the spatial dataset and tm_polygons() to render the polygon features, producing a choropleth map.
By default, tmap draws polygons with a dark gray outline (gray25) and a light gray fill (gray85).

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons()








4.2.2 Drawing a Choropleth Map Using tm_polygons()

Here is a summary of the key points of tm_polygons() defaults:
Classification: uses the “pretty” interval method.
Colour scheme: defaults to ColorBrewer’s Blues3 palette.
Missing values: shown in grey.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")








4.2.3 Drawing a Choropleth Map using tm_fill() and tm_borders()

tm_polygons() is essentially a convenient wrapper around two functions: tm_fill() and tm_borders().

tm_fill() controls how the interior of the polygons is coloured, typically applying a default colour palette to shade the areas based on data values.
tm_borders() draws the boundary lines of each polygon, adding the outlines of the shapefile to the choropleth map.

Therefore, `tm_polygons() performs both filling and outlining in a single step.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")








tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()







Borders in tm_borders(): by default, polygons are outlined in light gray.
fill_alpha: controls polygon transparency (0 = invisible, 1 = fully opaque).
Other key arguments:
col: border colour
lwd: border line width (default = 1, thin line)
lty: border line type (default = “solid”, others like dashed, dotted)

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")








4.3 Data Classification Methods of tmap
tmap supports ten data classification methods for choropleth mapping: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks.

4.3.1 Plotting Choropleth Maps with Built-in Classification Methods

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)







Quantile (above) shows differences more clearly, while Equal interval is better for showing absolute value ranges but may hide variation if data are skewed.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)







DIY 1: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "sd",
                n = 5)) +
    tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)  






tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5)) +
    tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)






tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "bclust",
                n = 5)) +
    tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

Committee Member: 1(1) 2(1) 3(1) 4(1) 5(1) 6(1) 7(1) 8(1) 9(1) 10(1)
Computing Hierarchical Clustering








DIY 2:
Using different class numbers changes map readability. Fewer classes (2–3) give a simple overview but hide variation. Moderate classes (5–7) balance detail and clarity. More classes (10–20) seem similar to 5-7 classes overall but too many classes could reduce clarity. So 5–7 classes are best for clear and insightful choropleth maps.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 2)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)






tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 6)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)






tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)






tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 20)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








4.3.2 Plotting Choropleth Map with Custom Break
For the built in classification styles in tmap, class intervals are calculated automatically. To override them, we can define our own intervals using the breaks argument in tm_fill().
The breaks vector must include both the minimum and maximum values. Therefore, to create n classes, n + 1 break values are required, arranged in increasing order.
Before choosing breakpoints, it is good practice to examine descriptive statistics of the variable. Based on the DEPENDENCY distribution, we set breakpoints at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80 and 0.90, and include the minimum and maximum values (0 and 1.00):
c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)
The choropleth map is then plotted using the code below.

summary(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.1111  0.7147  0.7867  0.8585  0.8763 19.0000      92 



tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








4.4 Colour Scheme
The tmap supports colour ramps that can be either user defined or selected from predefined palettes available in the RColorBrewer package.

4.4.1 Using ColourBrewer Palette
To change the colours, we assign the desired palette to the values argument in tm_scale_intervals(), as shown in the code below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)







Using “-” to reverse the colour shading.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








4.5 Map Layout
Map layout refers to the arrangement of all map elements into a cohesive map. These elements include the mapped features, title, scale bar, north arrow, margins, and aspect ratio.
The colour settings and data classification methods discussed earlier, such as palettes and breakpoints, influence the visual appearance of the map.

4.5.1 Map Legend
In tmap, the tm_legend() function provides several options to customise the legend’s placement, format, and appearance.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_pos_auto_in() +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type ="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone \n(Jenks classification)") +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left","bottom"))








4.5.2 Map style
tmap offers a wide range of layout settings that can be modified using tmap_style(), which icludes white (default), gray, natural, classic, cobalt, albatross, beaver, and bw (black & white).
The code chunk below applies the classic style.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tmap_style("natural")








#reset to default style; options: white (default), gray, natural, classic, cobalt, albatross, beaver, and bw (black & white).

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tmap_style("beaver")








4.5.3 Cartographic Furniture
The code chunk below uses tm_compass(), tm_scale_bar(), tm_grid() and tm_credit() to draw cartographic furniture like compass, scale bar, grid lines.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & Singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tmap_style("classic")







The code below resets the default style to “white”.

tmap_style("white")


4.6 Drawing Small Multiple (Facet) Choropleth Maps
Small multiple maps, also known as facet maps, consist of several maps arranged side by side and sometimes stacked vertically. They help visualise how spatial patterns vary with another variable, such as time.
In tmap, small multiple maps can be created in three ways:

assigning multiple values to at least one aesthetic argument,
specifying a grouping variable in tm_facets(), and
arranging separate maps using tmap_arrange().


4.6.1 By assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments
In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by specifying the ncols argument in tm_fill().

#{r} and use #| both can adjust the figure settings.
# assigning two variables to the visual variable (fill)
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) + 
  tm_polygons(
    fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
    fill.legend = 
      tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in(
        "right", "bottom"),
         ncol = 2),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal", 
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")








tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) + 
  tm_polygons(
    fill = c("DEPENDENCY", "AGED"),
    style = c("equal", "quantile"), 
    palette = list("Blues", "Greens")
  ) +
  tm_layout(
    fill.legend = tm_legend(position = tm_pos_out("right", "bottom"), ncol = 1),
    legend.position = c("right", "bottom")
  ) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)








4.6.2 By Defining a Group-by Variable in tm_facets()

The code below uses tm_facets() to split the map into facets by region name, arranged in 2 rows × 3 columns; each facet has its own coordinate system (free.coords), and subzones not in that facet are dropped (drop.units).
In R, c() stands for combine. It creates a vector by combining multiple values into one object.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) + 
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2, 
            ncols = 3,
            free.coords=TRUE, 
            drop.units=TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = TRUE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"), 
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








4.6.3 By Arranging Multiples Choropleth Maps with tmap_arrange()
In map_arrange(), asp controls the panel aspect ratio (height ÷ width): asp = 1 makes panels square, asp > 1 makes them taller than wide, asp < 1 makes them wider than tall, and asp = 0 allows free stretching. The ncol argument sets how many maps are placed per row.

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Young pPpulation")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Aged Population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp = 1, ncol = 2)

title: 08-1 Choropleth Mapping with R
section: 5 Mappping Spatial Object Meeting a Selection Criterion
text:
5 Mappping Spatial Object Meeting a Selection Criterion
Instead of creating small multiple choropleth maps, we can use a selection function to highlight only the spatial features that meet a specified criterion.

mpsz_pop2020 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020[mpsz_pop2020$REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION", ]) +
  tm_fill(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",
      values = "brewer.blues"
    ),
    fill.chart = tm_chart_histogram(),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      orientation = "portrait",
      position = tm_pos_out("right", "bottom")
    )
  ) +
  tm_layout(
    legend.height = 0.45,
    legend.width = 5.0,
    frame = FALSE
  ) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

title: 08-1 Choropleth Mapping with R
section: 6 Complementing Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
text:
6 Complementing Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
Legend charts are small charts that are added to the map, usually in addition to legends. Arguments that could be assigned to fill.chart are tm_chart_histogram(), tm_chart_bar(), tm_chart_donut(),tm_chart_violin(), tm_chart_box(), tm_chart_none(),tm_chart_heatmap().

mpsz_pop2020 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) + #other options 
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)








mpsz_selected <- mpsz_pop2020 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

stats <- boxplot.stats(mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY)

outlier_vals <- stats$out #$out gives the outlier values of DEPENDENCY (those outside 1.5×IQR rule).

outlier_sf <- mpsz_selected[mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tm_shape(mpsz_selected) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col ="red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_text("SUBZONE_N", col = "red", size = 0.7) +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)

title: 08-1 Choropleth Mapping with R
text:
7 Creating Interactive Map
Interactive maps (tmap_mode(“view”)) let users zoom, pan, and click for details.

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2020 %>%
  filter(REGION_N== "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected,
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N",
            "Dependnecy" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2)






The code chunk below adds tmap_mode(“plot”) after producing the interactive map to reset to static mode for subsequent maps.

tmap_mode("plot")

THe code chunk blow uses tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(12,14)) to control zoom freedom and keep the view focused.

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2020 %>%
  filter(REGION_N== "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected,
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N",
            "Dependnecy" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(12,14))







#reset to static maps
tmap_mode("plot")

title: 05-5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
In this hands-on exercise, we learn how to design treemaps using appropriate R packages.
The exercise is organised into three main sections.
First, we learn how to transform transaction data into a treemap structure using selected functions from the dplyr package.

3.3 Data Wrangling and Manipulation
The data frame realis2018 is in transaction record form, which is highly disaggregated and not suitable for treemap visualisation. In this section, we will prepare a summary data frame suitable for a treemap by completing two steps:
First, we group the transaction records by Project Name, Planning Region, Planning Area, Property Type, and Type of Sale. Next, we compute Total Units Sold, Total Area, Median Unit Price, and Median Transacted Price by applying appropriate summary statistics to No. of Units, Area (sqm), Unit Price ($ psm), and Transacted Price ($) respectively.
To do this, we will use two key verbs from dplyr: group_by() and summarise().
Grouping affects dplyr verbs in the following ways.

select() behaves the same as in an ungrouped data frame, except that grouping variables are always retained.
arrange() also behaves the same unless .by_group = TRUE is specified, in which case rows are ordered first by the grouping variables.
mutate() and filter() are most useful with window functions such as rank(), or expressions like min(x) == x.
sample_n() and sample_frac() take the specified number or fraction of rows within each group.
summarise() computes summary statistics for each group.

In our case, group_by() is used together with summarise() to produce a summarised data frame.






Tipdplyr Syntax




dplyr is an R package that provides a set of consistent and easy-to-use functions (called verbs) for data manipulation.
filter(): selects rows based on conditions; Syntax: filter(data, condition)
select(): selects columns by name or position; Syntax: select(data, column1, column2)
arrange(): reorders rows; Syntax: arrange(data, column)
mutate(): creates new variables or modifies existing ones; Syntax: mutate(data, new_col = expression)
summarise(): computes summary statistics; Syntax: summarise(data, summary = function(column))
group_by(): groups data so operations are applied within groups; Syntax: group_by(data, column)




3.4 Grouped Summaries without the Pipe
The code below shows the two steps approach to perform the aggregated calculation.
First, we use the group_by() function to group the data and then summerise() is used to calculate, and a grouped_df is created after the each code is executed.

realis2018_grouped <- group_by(realis2018, `Project Name`, `Planning Region`, `Planning Area`, `Property Type`,
                               `Type of Sale`)


realis2018_summarised <- summarise(realis2018_grouped, `Total Unit Sold`= sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   `Median Unit Price($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

The code chunk above is not very efficient because we have to assign a name to each intermediate data frame, even though we do not need to keep or reuse them.






Tip




Aggregation functions such as sum() and median() follow the usual rule for missing values: if any missing value is present in the input, the result will be NA. Setting the argument na.rm = TRUE removes missing values before the computation is performed.




3.5 Grouped summaries with the pipe

The code chunk below demonstrates a more efficient way to perform the same steps by using the pipe operator, %>%.
The pipe %>% passes the result of one operation directly into the next function, allowing multiple data manipulation steps to be written in a clear, sequential manner without creating intermediate data frames. This improves code readability and efficiency by expressing the workflow as a series of actions applied to the data from left to right.

realis2018_summarised <- realis2018 %>%
          group_by(`Project Name`, `Planning Region`, `Planning Area`, `Property Type`,
                               `Type of Sale`) %>%
  summarise(`Total Unit Sold`= sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
             `Median Unit Price($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
             `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

title: 05-5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
4 Designing Treemap with treemap Package
The treemap package is an R package designed to provide great flexibility for drawing treemaps. Its core function, treemap(), offers more than 43 arguments. In this section, we focus on the major arguments used to create treemaps that are both elegant and informative.

4.1 16.4.1 Designing a Static Treemap
In this section, treemap() from the treemap package is used to plot a treemap showing the distribution of median unit prices and total units sold for resale condominiums by geographical hierarchy in 2017.
First, we select records that belong to the resale condominium property type from the realis2018_selected data frame.

realis2018_selected <- realis2018_summarised %>%
  filter(`Property Type` == "Condominium", `Type of Sale` == "Resale")


4.2 Using the Basic Arguments
The code below demenstrates the use of core arguments of treemap(): index, vSize and vColor.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price ($ per sqm")













Important



Things to learn from the three arguments used:

index: the argument must contain at least two column names. Otherwise, a hierarchical treemap cannot be produced. When multiple column names are supplied, the order defines the hierarchy of the treemap. Planning Region forms the top level, Planning Area is nested within each region, and Project Name is nested within each planning area. This hierarchy determines how the treemap is subdivided.
vSize: the column specified in vSize must contain non-negative values only. This is because its values are used to determine the area of the rectangles in the treemap. Negative values cannot be mapped to rectangle sizes and will result in an invalid plot. Projects with more units sold occupy larger areas in the treemap. In other words, rectangle size represents sales volume.
vColor: controls the colour shading** of the rectangles. In general, darker colours indicate higher values, while lighter colours indicate lower values.









Warning




The treemap above is coloured incorrectly. In a well-designed treemap, rectangle colours should vary in intensity to represent the underlying quantitative variable, which in this case is the median unit price.
In treemap(), the vColor argument must be used together with the type argument to control how colours are assigned. If type is not explicitly specified, treemap() defaults to type = "index". This means the colours are mapped according to the hierarchical groups (for example, Planning Area) rather than the numeric values in vColor.
As a result, the rectangles are coloured by category instead of showing a colour gradient that reflects differences in median unit prices. To correctly represent prices using colour intensity, the type argument should be set appropriately, for example to indicate a value-based colour mapping rather than a hierarchy-based one.




4.3 Working with vColor and type Arguments
Here we pair the vColor argument with `type = “value”.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price ($ per sqm)"
       )  













Tip




The rectangles are coloured using different intensities of green to represent their respective median unit prices.
The legend shows that the values are grouped into ten bins, for example 0–5000, 5000–10000, and so on, with an equal interval of 5000 between bins.




4.4 Colours in treemap package
Two arguments control how colours are mapped in a treemap: mapping and palette. The key difference between "value" and "manual" lies in how the colour scale is applied by default.
When mapping = "value" is used, the treemap treats the palette as a diverging colour scheme (for example, ColorBrewer’s RdYlBu). The colours are mapped so that 0 corresponds to the midpoint colour (often white or yellow), −max(abs(values) maps to one end of the palette, and +max(abs(values)) maps to the other end. This approach is suitable when the data have a meaningful centre, such as positive and negative deviations.
In contrast, when mapping = "manual" is used, the colour mapping is based purely on the data range. The minimum value is mapped to the left end of the palette, the maximum value to the right end, and the midpoint of the range (the mean of the minimum and maximum) to the middle colour. This is more appropriate for variables such as prices or counts, where values are strictly non-negative and no natural zero-centred reference point exists.

4.5 The “value” type treemap
The code below introduces palette arugment.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        palette = "RdYlBu",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price ($ per sqm)"
       )  













Tip




Although the colour palette used is RdYlBu, there are no red rectangles in the treemap above because all median unit prices are positive. Under the default "value" mapping, the palette is centred at 0, so only the positive side of the diverging scale is used, which results in colours drawn mainly from one half of the palette rather than showing both extremes.
We only see about 5000 to 45000 in the legend because the range argument is, by default, set to c(min(values), max(values)), with “pretty” rounding applied to produce cleaner breakpoints for the legend.




4.6 The “manual” type treemap
The "manual" type does not interpret values in the same way as the "value" type. Instead, the data range is mapped linearly to the colour palette.
The code chunk below shows a treemap created using the "manual" type.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price($ psm)",
        type = "manual",
        palette = "RdYlBu",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price ($ per sqm)"
       )  













Tip



The colour scheme appears confusing because the default mapping is (min(values), mean(range(values)), max(values)). When all values are either positive or negative, using a diverging colour palette such as RdYlBu is not appropriate, as it implies a central reference point that does not exist in the data.


To address this issue, a sequential colour palette, such as Blues, should be used instead, as it provides a more intuitive representation of increasing or decreasing values.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price($ psm)",
        type = "manual",
        palette = "Blues",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price ($ per sqm)"
       )  








4.7 Treemap Layout
treemap() supports two commonly used treemap layouts: "squarified" and "pivotSize", with "pivotSize" as the default.
The squarified treemap algorithm (Bruls et al., 2000) aims to produce rectangles with good aspect ratios, making them easier to compare visually. However, it ignores the specified sorting order of the rectangles (sortID).
In contrast, the pivot-by-size (or "pivotSize") algorithm (Bederson et al., 2002) takes the sorting order (sortID) into account while still maintaining reasonably good aspect ratios. This makes it useful when both layout readability and ordering information are important.

4.8 Working with algorithm argument
The code chunk below plots a squarified treemap by changing the algorithm argument.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price($ psm)",
        type = "manual",
        palette = "Blues",
        algorithm = "squarified",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price ($ per sqm)"
       ) 








4.9 Using sortID
When the "pivotSize" algorithm is used, the sortID argument can be specified to determine the order in which rectangles are arranged, from the top left to the bottom right of the treemap.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price($ psm)",
        type = "manual",
        palette = "Blues",
        algorithm = "pivotSize",
        sortID = "Median Transacted Price",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price ($ per sqm)"
       )

title: 05-5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
5 Designing Treemap Using treemapify Package
Here we create a treemap using ggplot2 grammar and geom_treemap() from treemapify package.

ggplot(data = realis2018_selected,
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price($ psm)`))+
  geom_treemap(layout = "scol",start = "bottomleft") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightblue", high = "blue")













Tip




The area aesthetic determines the size of each rectangle, so projects with more units sold appear larger.
The fill aesthetic determines the colour of each rectangle, which represents the median unit price per square metre.
geom_treemap()
The layout algorithm, one of either “squarified” (the default), “scol”, “srow” or “fixed; scol (slice-and-dice by column) arranges rectangles in vertical slices to produce a simple and ordered layout.
start = "bottomleft" sets the starting position of the treemap layout to the bottom-left corner, which controls where the first rectangle is placed. One of ‘bottomleft’ (the default), ‘topleft’, ‘topright’ or ‘bottomright’.
scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightblue", high = "blue") This defines a sequential colour scale for the fill aesthetic. Lower median unit prices are shown in light blue, while higher prices are shown in darker blue.




5.1 Defining Hierarchy
Here we add subgroup to group the treemap by Planning region.

ggplot(data = realis2018_summarised,
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`)) +
  geom_treemap(start = "topleft") 







Here, we add darker borders to distinguish Planning Regions and lighter borders to delineate Planning Areas to create clearer visual separation between hierarchy.

ggplot(data = realis2018_summarised,
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`,
           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) +
  geom_treemap()+
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = "grey20") +
  geom_treemap_subgroup2_border(colour = "grey40", size = 2)

title: 05-5 Treemap Visualisation with R
text:
6 Designing Interactive Treemap using d3treeR

6.1 Installing d3treeR package
d3treeR package is not available on CRAN.
Here we install the package from GitHub by using remotes package. If remotes package is not installed, use intall.packages() function to install and library() to load the package, then use install_github() to install the package from Github and finally use library() to load the designated package.

install.packages("remotes")
library(remotes)
install_github("d3treeR/d3treeR")


library(d3treeR)


6.2 Designing An Interactive Treemap
The code below performs two main processes.
First, treemap() is used to construct a treemap using selected variables from the condominium data frame. The resulting treemap is saved as an object named tm.
Next, d3tree() is applied to the tm object to create an interactive treemap.

tm<- treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area"),
        vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
        vColor = "Median Unit Price($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price ($ per sqm)"
       ) 








d3tree(tm,rootname = "Singapore" )





Next we add tooltips to show more details.

tm_temp <- treemap(
  realis2018_summarised %>%
    mutate(
      temp_label = paste0(`Planning Area`, "\n($", 
                         round(`Median Unit Price($ psm)`/1000, 1), "K psm)")
    ),
  index = c("Planning Region", "temp_label"),
  vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
  vColor = "Median Unit Price($ psm)",
  type = "value",
  title = "Private Residential Property Sold, 2017",
  title.legend = "Median Unit Price ($ per sqm)"
)








d3tree(tm_temp,
       rootname = "Singapore")





The tooltips appear cluttered and are not very informative.
Heatmaps shows the hieachical structure but may not be the best choice for interactive visualisation, as they often lack granularity. Other chart types, such as interactive maps, can provide clearer insights and more precise comparisons.

title: 05-4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
Parallel coordinates plots are designed for visualising and analysing multivariate numerical data. They allow multiple variables to be compared at once and help reveal relationships, such as factors contributing to a Happiness Index. The technique was introduced by Alfred Inselberg in the 1970s and is more common in academic and scientific settings than business reporting. As Stephen Few (2006) notes, parallel coordinates are most effective as an interactive tool for uncovering multivariate patterns.
We will learn how to create static parallel coordinates plots using ggparcoord() from GGally, and interactive parallel coordinates plots using the parallelPlot package.

text:
4 Plotting Static Parallel Coordinates Plot
ggparcoord() from GGally package is used to create static arallel coordinates plot.

4.1 Key Arguments

data: the data.frame to plot.
columns : which variables (names or indices) become the parallel axes.
groupColumn : a variable (e.g. region) to colour (group) the lines by.
scale : how to scale variables (e.g., "std", "uniminmax"(min 0, max 1), "globalminmax", "robust").
scaleSummary : summary statistic used when centring (scale = "center").
centerObsID : observation to centre on when scale = "centerObs".
missing : how to handle missing values ("exclude", "random", etc.).
order : how to order the axes (can be a custom order or methods like "anyClass").
showPoints : if TRUE, adds points at each variable value.
splineFactor : whether to smooth lines using splines.
alphaLines : transparency (or a column name for per-line alpha) for the lines ( 0 -1).
boxplot / shadeBox : show boxplots or shaded ranges under each axis (TRUE or FALSE).
mapping : additional ggplot2::aes() mappings passed to the plot.
title : plot title.

4.2 Plotting a simple parallel coordinates plot
The code below creates a basic static parrallel coordinators plot based on columns 7 to 12.

ggparcoord(data = wh, columns = c(7:12))








4.3 Plotting a parallel coordinates with boxplot
The basic parallel coordinates plot did not provide a meaningful interpretation of the World Happiness indicators. Next we improve the plot but adding a range of arguments available in ggparcoord().

ggparcoord(data = wh, columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happines Variables")

title: 05-1 Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
Ternary plots visualise three part compositional data, such as population age structure (elderly, economical active and young population) or soil composition(sand, slit and clay). They are shown as a triangle scaled from 0 to 1 on each side, with each side representing one component. A point’s position reflects the proportions of all three components.
In this hands on exercise, we use R to build ternary plots to analyse Singapore’s population structure. The steps are 1. to load the required packages tidyverse and ggtern, 2. derive three measures using mutate() from dplyr, 3. create a static ternary plot with ggtern() from ggtern package, 4. and then build an interactive version using Plotly package.

3 Data Preparation

3.1 The Data
For this hands on exercise, the dataset Singapore Residents by Planning Area Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling, June 2000–2018 will be used. The data has already been downloaded and saved in the data sub-folder of the exercise directory as a CSV file named respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv.

3.2 Importing the Data
The code below uses read_csv() from readr package to import the dataset into R environment.

pop_data <- read_csv("data/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv")

The preview table displays the first six records of the dataset. It contains five columns, where PA, SZ, and AG are categorical variables, while Year and Population are numeric variables of type double.

3.3 Preparing the Data
The mutate() function of dplyr package derives three new measures, namely: young, active, and old as shown below.
The spread(AG, Population) of tidyr package converts the data from long to wide format by turning AG values into columns and filling them with Population values.

agpop_mutated <- pop_data %>%
  mutate(`Year` = as.character(Year)) %>%
  spread(AG, Population) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[4:8]))%>%
  mutate(ACTIVE = rowSums(.[9:16]))  %>%
  mutate(OLD = rowSums(.[17:21])) %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = rowSums(.[22:24])) %>%
  filter(Year == 2018)%>%
  filter(TOTAL > 0)

title: 05-1 Creating Ternary Plot with R
text:
4 Plotting Ternary Diagram with R

4.1 Plotting a static ternary diagram
Here we use ggtern() function of ggtern package to create a simple ternary plot.
ggtern() creates a ternary plot for the YOUNG, ACTIVE, and OLD age groups, while geom_point() displays their proportions as points within the triangle.

ggtern(data=agpop_mutated,aes(x=YOUNG,y=ACTIVE, z=OLD)) +
  geom_point()







The code below adds a title to the ternary plot using labs(). The theme_rgbw() function applies a clean black and white theme with coloured ternary axes in red, green, and blue to represent the three components, while keeping the background white.

ggtern(data=agpop_mutated, aes(x=YOUNG,y=ACTIVE, z=OLD)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title="Population structure, 2018") +
  theme_rgbw()








4.2 Plotting an interative ternary diagram
The code below creates an interactive ternary plot using plot_ly() function of Plotly.
we first create a reusable function for adding annotations to plots and returns a list of annotation settings. The annotation is positioned Positions at top left (x = 0.1 and y = 1: 10% from left, 100% from bottom) by using relative coordinates (xref/yref = "paper") . Styling is applied with a white serif font on a grey background and a black border.

label <- function(txt) {
  list(
    text = txt,
    x = 0.1, y = 1,
    ax = 0, ay = 0,
    xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
    align = "center",
    font = list(family = "serif", size = 15, colour = "white"),
    bgcolour = "#b3b3b3", bordercolour = "black", borderwidth = 2
  )
}

Next we create axis formatting function. tickformat = ".0%" formats tick labels as percentages with 0 decimal places. we then set font size to 10 for axis labels.

axis <- function(txt){
  list(
    title = txt, tickformat = ".0%", tickfont = list(size = 10)
  )
}

The code below defines the three axes for the ternary plot. Each axis gets a label and the formatting from theaxis() function. In ternary plots: a + b + c = 1 (or 100%).

ternaryAxes <- list(
  aaxis = axis("Young"),
  baxis = axis("Active"),
  caxis = axis("Old")
)

The code below creates the ternary plot by mapping Young to ‘a’ axis, Active to b’ axis (Active) and Old to c’ axis, sets colour parameter: scatterternary uses marker = list(color = ...) instead of color = I(“black”), specifies ternary scatter plot type and add layout configurations.

plot_ly(
  agpop_mutated,
  a = ~YOUNG,  
  b = ~ACTIVE,
  c = ~OLD,
  type = "scatterternary",
  mode = "markers",
  marker = list(color = "black")
) %>%
  layout(
    annotations = label("Population Structure, 2018"),
    ternary = ternaryAxes
  )






pp<- plot_ly(
  agpop_mutated,
  a = ~YOUNG,  
  b = ~ACTIVE,
  c = ~OLD,
  type = "scatterternary",
  mode = "markers",
  marker = list(
    color = "blue",
    line = list(
      color = "grey50",  # Border colour
      width = 1          # Border width
    ),
    size = 8,
    opacity = 0.7
  )
) %>%
   layout(
    annotations = label("Population Structure, 2018"),
    ternary = ternaryAxes
  )

pp





Here we create an animated ternary plot using population data from 2000 to 2018. We can also create animated ternary plot showing population development in each PA over the years by using color = ~PA.

agpop <- pop_data %>%
  mutate(`Year` = as.character(Year)) %>%
  spread(AG, Population) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[4:8]))%>%
  mutate(ACTIVE = rowSums(.[9:16]))  %>%
  mutate(OLD = rowSums(.[17:21])) %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = rowSums(.[22:24])) %>%
  filter(TOTAL > 0)


# create the plot
p <- plot_ly(
  agpop, 
  a = ~YOUNG, 
  b = ~ACTIVE, 
  c = ~OLD, 
  frame = ~Year,
  type = "scatterternary",
  mode = "markers",
  sizes = c(5, 30)               
) %>%
  layout(
    ternary = ternaryAxes
  )

# add dynamic title via frames
# access the animation frames in the plot object

p$x$frames <- lapply(p$x$frames, function(frame) {
  #adds title to each frame's layout
  frame$layout$title <- list(
    # each frame has a "name" (the Year value)
    text = paste("Population by Year:", frame$name),
    # title location
    x = 0.1, y = 0.95
  )
  frame
})

# Add initial title to show title for first frame before animation starts
# access the main plot layout
p$x$layout$title <- list(
  #gGets the smallest year value
  text = paste("Population by Year:", min(agpop$Year)),
  x = 0.1, y = 0.95
)

# Add animation controls
p <- p %>%
  animation_opts(
    #each frame displays for 1 second
    frame = 1000,
    # transition between frames 0.5s
    transition = 500,
    # smooth linear transition
    easing = "linear"
  ) %>%
  #adds the year slider
  animation_slider(
    #shows Year: year value
    currentvalue = list(prefix = "Year: ")
  )

p





$x is plotly’s internal storage for the plot specification.

pp$x

title: 04-3 Visualising Uncertainty
text:
Visualising uncertainty is a relatively recent development in statistical graphics. In this chapter, we learn how to create uncertainty visualisations, including error bars with ggplot2, interactive plots with plotly and DT, advanced graphics with ggdist, and hypothetical outcome plots (HOPs) using ungeviz.
Assumption:
All hypothesis tests in this exercise are conducted at the 5% significance level, where the null hypothesis states that no significant difference or no relationship exists between the variables of interest.

2 Getting Started

2.1 Installing and Loading the Required Libraries
There are four packages that will be used in this exercise.


Package
Description



tidyverse
A collection of R packages for data importing, cleaning, transformation, and visualisation (e.g., readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2).


ggdist
An R package that extends ggplot2 with flexible geoms and stats for visualising distributions and uncertainty.


gganimate
The ggplot2 extension used to create animated statistical graphs.


plotly
Creates interactive and publication-ready graphs.


DT
Displays data frames as interactive HTML tables with sorting, filtering, and pagination.


crosstalk
An extension of the htmlwidgets package that provides classes, functions, and conventions to enable cross-widget interactions, such as linked brushing and filtering, across multiple interactive widgets.


colorspace
Provides tools for selecting, manipulating and applying colours and colour palettes in data visualisations.


ggridges
A gglot extension that creates ridgeline plots to visualise the changes in distributions over time or space.



The code below installs and loads the required packages into R environment.

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, ggdist, gganimate, plotly, DT, crosstalk, colorspace, ggridges)


2.2 Importing the Data
A CSV file containing the final exam results of 322 local Primary 3 students has been imported into the R environment by using function read_csv() from readr package, one of tidyverse family. The dataset includes variables such as student ID, class, gender, race, and grades for English, Maths, and Science.

section: 3 Visualising the Uncertainty of Point Estimates: ggplot2 Methods
text:
3 Visualising the Uncertainty of Point Estimates: ggplot2 Methods
A point estimate is a single value, such as a mean, whereas uncertainty is expressed using measures like the standard error, confidence interval, or credible interval.






Important



Do not confuse the uncertainty of a point estimate with the variability in the sample.


In this section, we will learn how to plot error bars for Maths scores by race using the exam tibble. First, the code chunk below is used to compute the required summary statistics.

my_sum <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(n= n(),             # compute the sample size for each race group
            mean = mean(MATHS), # calculate the mean Maths score for each group
            sd = sd(MATHS)) %>% # calculate the standard deviation
  mutate(se = sd/sqrt(n-1))     # compute the standard error of the mean







TipThings to learn from the code chunk above



The group_by() function from dplyr groups observations by race, summarise() computes the sample size, mean, and standard deviation of Maths scores, and mutate() derives the standard error for each race group. The results are stored in a tibble called my_sum.








Note



For the mathematical explanation, please refer to Slide 20 of Lesson 4.


The table below displays my_sum tibble data frame in an html format.
