title: 02 Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2 Getting Started

2.1 Installing and Loading the Required Libraries
There are five packages that will be used in this exercise.


Package
Description



tidyverse
A collection of R packages for data importing, cleaning, transformation, and visualisation (e.g., readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2).


ggrepel
Provides geoms for non-overlapping text labels in ggplot2


ggthemes
Provides ggplot2 themes, geoms and scales that replicate the famous styles ( e.g. Tufte, Economist, Tufte)


hrbrthemes
Provides minimal and professional looking themes and better typography and styleing


patchwork
Extends ggplot2 by letting user combine plots easily using operators.



The code below installs and loads the required packages into R environment. hrbrthemes package can be installed using the remote package, the code can be found on its github ReadMe.

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, ggrepel, ggthemes, hrbrthemes, patchwork)

The code chunk below solves the system warning when using hrbthemes on Windows.

extrafont::loadfonts(device = "all") # quiet = TRUE


2.2 Importing the Data
A CSV file containing the final exam results of 322 local Primary 3 students has been imported into the R environment by using function read_csv() from readr package, one of tidyverse family. The dataset includes variables such as student ID, class, gender, race, and grades for English, Maths, and Science.

exam_data <- read_csv("data/Exam_data.csv")

title: 02 Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
3 Beyond ggplot2 Annotation: ggrepel
To visualise the Maths and English scores for each student in a scatterplot, we can use geom_point() and geom_smooth() to add a reference line. However since all the student IDs are shown on the chart, the labels overlap and become difficult to read.


The plot
The code














ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
         geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth  = 0.5) +
  geom_label(aes(label = ID, hjust = 0.5, vjust= -0.5)) + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim = c(0,100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores VS Math scores for Primary 3")




Here we could use functions like geom_text_repel() or geom_label_repel() from ggrepel package to customise the label geoms for ggplot2. The difference is that geom_label_repel() adds a rectangle behind the text, which helps the labels stand out from the background, similar to geom_label() vs geom_text() that it shows plain text only.

3.1 Working with ggrepel
ggrepel automatically places labels nicely to minimise overlap. However, we can still force all labels to be displayed by using the argument max.overlaps = Inf. The text font can be adjusted using the family argument, while the font style can be changed using fontface. In addition,box.padding controls the spacing between labels, the smaller the value, the closer the labels will be.


The plot - label
The code - label
The plot - text
The code - text














ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
         geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth  = 0.5) +
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = ID, fontface = "bold")) + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim = c(0,100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores VS Math scores for Primary 3")














ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
         geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth  = 0.5) +
   geom_text_repel(aes(label = ID), 
                  family = "serif", box.padding = 0.5)+
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim = c(0,100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores VS Math scores for Primary 3")

title: 02 Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
4 Beyond ggplot2 Themes: ggthemes
There are 8 built-in themes in ggplot2. They are: theme_gray()(default), theme_bw(), theme_classic(), theme_dark(), theme_light(), theme_linedraw(), theme_minimal(), and theme_void(), some of them we tried out in Hand-on Exercise 1.11.


The plot - linedraw
The plot - dark
The plot - blackwhite
The plot - void




VIEW CODEggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= GENDER, y =MATHS, colour = GENDER)) +
         geom_violin() +
  ggtitle("Maths scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_linedraw()










VIEW CODEggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_violin(trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggtitle("Maths scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_dark()










VIEW CODEggplot(exam_data, aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS, fill = RACE)) +
  geom_violin(trim = FALSE, alpha = 0.6, width = 0.8) +
  ggtitle("Maths scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_bw()










VIEW CODEggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
         geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100, fill = "lightblue", colour = "grey25") +
  ggtitle("Maths scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_void()











4.1 Working with ggtheme Package
ggthemes mimics famous plotting styles such as The Wall Street Journal theme_wsj(), The Economist theme_economist(), Stata theme_stata(), Excel theme_excel(), Edward Tufte theme_tufte(), Stephen Few theme_few(), and FiveThirtyEighttheme_fivethirtyeight().
Here we try all out again.


Stata
The Economist
Excel
The WSJ
Tufte
Few
FiveThirtyEight




VIEW CODEggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
         geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100, fill = "lightblue", colour = "grey25") +
  ggtitle("Maths Scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_stata()










VIEW CODEggplot(exam_data, aes(x = RACE, y = MATHS, fill = RACE)) +
  geom_violin() +
  coord_flip() +
  ggtitle("Maths Scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_economist()










VIEW CODEggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
         geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100, fill = "lightblue", colour = "grey25") +
  ggtitle("Maths scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_excel()










VIEW CODEexam_data %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(mean_maths = mean(MATHS, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_maths, y = reorder(RACE, mean_maths))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100)) +
  ggtitle("Average Maths Scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_wsj() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16))










VIEW CODEggplot(exam_data, aes(x = GENDER, y = MATHS, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_violin(trim = FALSE, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.3) +
  ggtitle("Maths scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_tufte()










VIEW CODEggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
         geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100, fill = "lightblue", colour = "grey25") +
  ggtitle("Maths scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_few()










VIEW CODEggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
         geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100, fill = "lightblue", colour = "grey25") +
  ggtitle("Maths scores for Primary 3") +
  theme_fivethirtyeight()











4.2 Working with hrbthemes Package
hrbthemes provides typographic themes and components for ggplot2 e.g. themes(theme_ipsum()), scales (scale_y_percent()), palettes(ft_cols()), fonts(font_ps()), Bit12 colour scales (scale_fill_bit12_continuous()), Flexoki palettes (flexoki_light()), utilities (flush_ticks()).


theme_ipsum()
theme_ipsum() with Styling




VIEW CODEsysfonts::font_add_google("PT Sans Narrow", "PT Sans Narrow")
showtext::showtext_auto()
ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100,
                 colour = "grey25", fill = "grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths Scores")+
   theme_ipsum(base_family = "PT Sans Narrow")









The hrbrthemes package has two main goals: improving typography in plots (such as label placement and fonts) and supporting efficient production workflows.
A production workflow refers to creating visuals for publication, such as blog posts, papers, reports, or presentations. While rough plots are useful during analysis, polished final graphics can help capture attention and improve audience engagement.

VIEW CODEggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100, color="grey25", 
                 fill="grey90") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Maths Scores", caption = "Primary 3 students' year-end scores") +
  theme_ipsum(base_family = "PT Sans Narrow", axis_title_size = 18,
              base_size = 15,
              grid = "Y")
















TipTips




axis_title_size controls the axis title font size
base_size Sets the default text size for the theme
grid Controls whether grid lines appear. If set to “Y”, it shows grid lines mainly to help track values along the y-axis (making it easier to compare heights/levels).
base_family is used to set the font family. On Windows, the default fonts used by theme_ipsum() (Arial Narrow) and theme_ft_rc() (Roboto Condensed) may not be installed, which causes warning messages. If base_family is not specified, R will fall back to the default sans font. However, we can use font_import() from extrafont package to import the fonts from system fonts folder to a R font database (the process might take a few minutes) and then load the fonts into the R environment by using loadfonts(device = "win"). Alternatively, we use font_add_google() from sysfonts package to download the fonts and load the fonts using showtext_auto() from showtext package.

title: 02 Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
5 Beyond Single Graph
We usually need multiple graphs to tell a compelling visual story. Several ggplot2 extensions provide functions for composing figures made up of multiple plots. In this section, we learn how to create a composite plot by combining multiple graphs. First, let us create three statistical graphics using the code chunk below.


p1
p2
p3




VIEW CODEp1<- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x=MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100,
                 colour = "grey25", fill = "grey90") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100)) + 
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths Scores")

p1










VIEW CODEp2<- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100,
                 colour = "grey25", fill = "grey90") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100)) + 
  ggtitle("Distribution of English Scores")

p2










VIEW CODEp3<- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x=MATHS, y =ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth= 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim = c(0,100)) + 
  ggtitle("English Scores versus Maths Scores for Primary 3")

p3











5.1 Creating Composite Graphics: pathwork Methods
Several ggplot2 extension packages support composite figures, such as grid.arrange() from gridExtra package and plot_grid() from cowplot. In this section, we learn patchwork, a ggplot2 extension designed to combine multiple ggplot2 plots into one figure.

Patchwork has a simple syntax:




+ arranges plots side by side





() groups plots





/ stacks plots vertically



5.2 Combining Two ggplot2 Graphs
The tabset below shows two histograms combined using patchwork by using +. The syntax is simple and intuitive.


Left & right
Top & bottom




VIEW CODEp1 + p2










VIEW CODEp1 / p2











5.3 Combining Three ggplot2 Graphs
More complex composite plots can be created using patchwork operators. For example, the figure below uses / to stack plots, | to place plots side by side, and () to control the layout order.
Further examples can be found on plot Assembly.


Three graphs
Graph with table




VIEW CODE(p1 / p2) | p3









Here, wrap_table() from patchwork is used to create a table. A similar result can also be achieved using gt() from the gt package.

VIEW CODEp3 + wrap_table(exam_data[1:10, c("MATHS", "ENGLISH")], panel = "full", space = "fixed") 











5.4 Creating a Composite Figure with Tag
To help reference subplots in the text, patchwork also supports auto-tagging, as shown in the figure below. Auto-tagging can be enabled by setting tag_levels in plot_annotation() to specify the tag style: '1' for Arabic numerals, 'A' for uppercase letters, 'a' for lowercase letters, 'I' for uppercase Roman numerals, and 'i' for lowercase Roman numerals.


Simple tagging
Tag with prefix and suffix




VIEW CODE((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels = "I",
    caption = "Disclaimer: These plots are mainly for practice.")










VIEW CODE((p1 / p2) | p3) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = c('A', '1'), tag_prefix = 'Fig. ',
                                 tag_sep = '.', tag_suffix = ':',caption = "Disclaimer: These plots are mainly for practice.")











5.5 Creating Figure with Insert
Besides arranging plots using predefined layouts, we could use inset_element() from pacthwork to place one or more plots or graphical elements freely on top of, or within, another plot.






TipKey arguments for inset_element()




p: object to inset (ggplot/grob/gt/etc.)
left, bottom, right, top: inset position (numeric or unit)
align_to: reference area (“panel” (default), “plot”, “full”)
on_top: place inset above or below the main plot
clip: clip inset to bounds or not
ignore_tag: exclude inset from auto-tagging





Basic use
Alignment
Tagging



Tip: keep values between 0 and 1 (npc units) and always ensure left < right, bottom < top.

VIEW CODEp3 + inset_element(p2, 
                   left = 0.02, 
                   bottom = 0.7, 
                   right = 0.5, 
                   top = 1)










VIEW CODEp3 + inset_element(p2, 
                   left = 0.5, 
                   bottom = 0.05, 
                   right = 1, 
                   top = 0.3,
                   align_to = "plot")










VIEW CODEp3 + inset_element(p2, 0.5, 0.05, 1, 0.3, align_to= "plot",ignore_tag= TRUE) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = '1',  caption = "Demenstration only")











5.6 Creating a Composite Figure by Using patchwork and ggtheme


ggthemes
Built-in themes
hrbthemes



Figure below is created by combining patchwork and theme_economist() of ggthemes package using operator &, applying to all plots in the patchwork layout. If you use + , the theme is applied only to the last patchwork object, not every subplot.

VIEW CODEpatchwork <- p3 / (p1 + p2) 
patchwork & theme_economist()










VIEW CODEpatchwork <- (p1 / p2) | p3
patchwork & theme_linedraw()

title: 03-2 Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R
text:
Animated graphics often engage audiences more effectively than static visuals. In this exercise, we will create animated visualisations using gganimate and plotly, and practise data reshaping with tidyr and data wrangling with dplyr.


Animations do not involve a moving plot. They are created by stitching together many static plots, each built from a different subset of the data, to create the illusion of motion.

Before creating an animated graph, it helps to understand two basics.
A frame is a single snapshot of data at a given time or category.
Animation attributes control how the frames transition and how long they appear.






Tip



Use animation thoughtfully. It is often unnecessary for exploration, but can be powerful in presentations when used sparingly. As seen in Hans Rosling’s TED talks, animation makes patterns clearer and more memorable.

2 Getting Started

2.1 Installing and Loading the Required Libraries
There are five packages that will be used in this exercise.


Package
Description



tidyverse
A collection of R packages for data importing, cleaning, transformation, and visualisation (e.g., readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2).


gganimate
The ggplot2 extension used to create animated statistical graphs.


gifski
A rendering engine used by gganimate to turn animation frames into high quality GIFs. It handles the final export, not the animation logic itself.


plotly
Creates interactive and publication-ready graphs.


gapminder
A dataset and visualisation concept popularised by Hans Rosling. In ggplot and gganimate, Gapminder data is often used as an example to demonstrate animated plots over time, such as countries moving across income and life expectancy.Used here solely to apply its country color scheme.

Tip

In the original approach, mutate_each() was used to convert all character variables to factors. However, mutate_each_() was deprecated in dplyr 0.7.0 and funs() was deprecated in dplyr 0.8.0. As a result, the code was rewritten using mutate_at(). In more recent versions of dplyr, the same outcome can be achieved using across(), which is now the recommended and more commonly used approach, its syntax: across(.cols, .fns).

title: 03-2 Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R
text:
3 Animated Data Visualisation: gganimate Methods
gganimate builds on ggplot2’s grammar of graphics by adding animation specific components that describe how a plot evolves over time. These components are added to a ggplot object to control different animation behaviours.

transition_*() controls how data is mapped across time and how observations relate between frames.
view_*() specifies how positional scales change during the animation.
shadow_*() defines how data from other time points is shown in the current frame.
enter_*() and exit_*() control how new data appears and old data disappears.
ease_aes() determines how aesthetic changes are smoothed between transitions.


3.1 Building a Static Population Bubble Plot
This code builds a bubble scatter plot that is designed to be animated.

ggplot(globalPop, aes(x = Old, y = Young, size = Population, color = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) + #controls the minimum and maximum sizes of the bubbles
  labs(title = 'Year: {frame_time}',
       x = '% Aged', y = '% Young')








3.2 Building the Animated Bubble Plot
In the code chunk below, transition_time() from gganimate is used to create transitions across distinct time states, in this case the Year variable. The ease_aes() function controls how aesthetic changes are smoothed between frames. While the default easing is linear, other options include quadratic, cubic, quartic, quintic, sine, circular, exponential, elastic, back, and bounce.
In the animated bubble plot, the bubbles show how countries move over time, shifting from a higher percentage of young population toward a higher percentage of aged population.

ggplot(globalPop, aes(x = Old, y = Young, size = Population, color = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) + #controls the minimum and maximum sizes of the bubbles
  labs(title = 'Year: {frame_time}',
       x = '% Aged', y = '% Young')+
  transition_time(Year) +
  ease_aes('linear')

title: 03-2 Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R
text:
4 Animated Data Visualisation: plotly
In the Plotly R package, both ggplotly() and plot_ly() allow key frame animations using the frame argument or aesthetic. They also provide an ids argument or aesthetic to maintain object constancy, ensuring smoother transitions for elements with the same identifier across frames.

4.1 Building an Animated Bubble plot: ggplotly()
In this subsection, we learn how to create an animated bubble plot using the ggplotly() method. Appropriate ggplot2 functions are first used to create a static bubble plot, and the output is saved as an R object called gg. The ggplotly() function is then applied to convert this R graphic object into an animated SVG object.
Unlike gganimate, which uses transition_time(Year), Plotly creates animations by specifying frame = Year. The animated bubble plot includes play and pause controls as well as a slider for controlling the animation. Note that even when show.legend = FALSE is specified, the legend may still appear. To fully remove it, theme(legend.position = "none") should be used, as shown in the plot and code chunk below.
ggplotly() is not a native animation solution, it is a conversion layer with partial animation support.

gg <- ggplot(globalPop, 
       aes(x = Old, 
           y = Young, 
           size = Population, 
           colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = Population,
                 frame = Year),
             alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(x = '% Aged', 
       y = '% Young') + 
  theme(legend.position='none')

ggplotly(gg)






4.2 Building an Animated Bubble Plot: plot_ly()
It’s not that plot_ly “always” uses ~, but it’s strongly recommended when working with data frames.

bp <- plot_ly(
  data = globalPop,
  x = ~Old, y = ~Young,
  frame = ~Year,
  ids = ~Country,
  type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
  size = ~Population,
  sizes = c(2, 100),
  color = ~Continent,
  text = ~Country,
  hoverinfo = "text",
  marker = list(line = list(width = 0))
) %>%
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "% Aged"),
    yaxis = list(title = "% Young"),
    showlegend = FALSE)


bp

5 Cherry Blossom Front
Sakura zensen is a Japanese term referring to the “front line” of cherry blossom blooming. Each spring, when cherry blossoms reach their peak bloom, known as mankai, people gather to enjoy hanami, the tradition of flower viewing. title: 04-2 Visual Statistical Analysis
text:
3 Visual Statistical Analysis with ggstatsplot
ggstatsplot is an extension of ggplot2 that creates information-rich graphics by embedding statistical test results directly into plots. It provides alternative inference methods by default and follows APA best-practice standards for statistical reporting.







TipMarkdown tips




_ is for subscripts
{} groups text or numbers
 keeps words readable in subscripts
Always wrap math in $ … $




3.1 One-sample test: gghistostats() method
The code below displays a histogram for a one-sample test of the English score distribution using gghistostats(), which runs the test automatically when type = "bayes" is selected. In this context, test.value specifies the reference value being tested, that is, the value the English scores are compared against. The plot itself displays the MAP (Maximum A Posteriori) estimate, which represents the most probable value of the parameter given the data and the prior.
The type argument supports four options: parametric, nonparametric, robust, and bayes. We can specify any option using just its first letter.
The ggtheme argument allows the user to apply a ggplot2 theme to the plot. The default is theme_ggstatsplot(), but any ggplot2 theme or themes from extension packages, such as theme_bw(), theme_fivethirtyeight() from ggthemes or theme_ipsum_ps() from hrbrthemes package , can be used.

SHOWset.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores")













TipPosterior summary




Posterior difference = 7.16, estimated difference between the sample mean and the test.value. The English scores are estimated to be about 7.16 points higher than the value being tested.
95% ETI [5.54, 8.75], 95% credible interval for the difference. There is a 95% probability that the true difference lies between 5.54 and 8.75.
\(\log_e(BF_{01})\) = −31.45, the log Bayes Factor comparing the null hypothesis to the alternative. A large negative value indicates extremely strong evidence against the null hypothesis.
\(r_{\substack{\text{JZS} \\ \text{Cauchy}}}\) = 0.71, the scale of the Cauchy prior used in the Bayesian test.




3.1.1 Unpacking the bayes factor

A Bayes factor compares how well two competing hypotheses explain the observed data. It is defined as the ratio of the likelihood of one hypothesis to that of another and is commonly interpreted as the strength of evidence in favour of one theory over the other.
Because the Bayes factor evaluates evidence for both the null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) and the alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)), it allows direct comparison between them while also incorporating prior or external information. When comparing(\(H_1\)) to (\(H_0\)), the Bayes factor is usually written as \(BF_{01}\).
The Schwarz criterion (also known as the Bayesian Information Criterion, BIC) provides a simple way to obtain a rough approximation of the Bayes factor.



3.1.2 How to interpret Bayes Factor
A Bayes factor can take any positive value. One widely used interpretation, first proposed by Harold Jeffreys (1961) and later refined by Lee and Wagenmakers (2012), categorises Bayes factors into ranges that indicate the strength of evidence for one hypothesis over another.

The table is written for \(BF_{10}\) (evidence for \(H_1\) over \(H_0\)).

Values greater than 1 favour \(H_1\)
Values less than 1 favour \(H_0\)

In ggstatsplot outputs, the reported quantity is: \(log_e(BF_{01})\), where \(BF_{01}\) represents evidence for \(H_0\) relative to \(H_1\), namely the inverse of \(BF_{10}\).
Mathematically, \(log_e(BF_{01})\) = - \(log_e(BF_{10})\)
Interpretation:






Value of \(log_e(BF_{01})\)

Implication



\(>4.6\)
Extreme evidence for \(H_0\)



\(>2.3\)
Strong evidence for \(H_0\)



\(>1\)
Moderate Evidence for \(H_0\)



\(>0\)
Week evidence for \(H_0\)



\(=0\)
No evidence (BF = 1)


\(<0\)
Week evidence for \(H_1\)



\(<-1\)
Moderate evidence for \(H_1\)



\(< -2.3\)
Strong Evidence for \(H_1\)



\(<-4.6\)
Extreme evidence for \(H_1\)










Important



Since test.value is 60, then:
\(H_0\): The true mean English score is 60.
\(H_1\): The true mean English score is not 60.
The data provide very strong Bayesian evidence that the true average English score is higher than the value being tested, with the most probable value around 75.



3.2 Two-sample mean test: ggbetweenstats()
In the code chunk below, ggbetweenstats() is used to create a visualisation for a two-sample mean test comparing Maths scores by gender.

SHOWggbetweenstats(data = exam, x = GENDER, y = MATHS,
               type = "np", message = FALSE)+
  labs(title = "Two-sample mean test comparing Maths scores by gender") +
  hrbrthemes::theme_ipsum_rc(grid="Y")













TipWhat we learnt from the chart?




Distributions: each group (Female and Male) is shown using a violin plot, which displays the full distribution of Maths scores. The width of the violin indicates where scores are more concentrated. Both distributions are slightly left skewed.
Boxplots: inside each violin is a boxplot, summarising the median and interquartile range. This helps compare central tendency and spread between genders.
Individual observations: jittered dots represent individual students, making it easy to see sample size and score dispersion.
Central tendency markers: the red dot marks the estimated median for each group, labelled directly on the plot (Female = 74, Male = 75).
Test statistic and p-value: A Mann–Whitney U test (non-parametric two-sample test) is reported at the top of the chart. \(W\)=13011.00, \(p\)=0.91. The p-value (greater than 0.05) indicates no statistically significant difference in Maths scores between female and male students.
Effect size : the rank-biserial correlation 0.007 which is extremely small, with a 95% confidence interval of \([−0.12,0.13]\). This suggests a negligible effect size.
Sample sizes are shown below each group label: Female \(n\)=170, Male \(n\)=152, with a total \(n_{obs}\)=322.
Summary: Although male students have a slightly higher median score (75 vs 74), the distributions overlap heavily, the effect size is close to zero, and the statistical test provides no evidence of a meaningful difference.




3.3 One-way ANOVA Test: ggbetweenstats() method
In the code chunk below,ggbetweenstats()is used to build a visual for One-way ANOVA test on English score by race.

SHOWggbetweenstats(data = exam, x = RACE, y = MATHS,
               type = "p", mean.ci = TRUE,
               pairwise.display = "s",
               p.adjust.method = "fdr",
               messages = FALSE)













TipWhat we learnt from the example?




pairwise.display: “s”: only significant, shows only statistically significant pairwise comparisons between groups. Others like “ns”: only non-significant; “all”: everything
type = "p" requests a parametric test. Since there are more than two groups, this results in a Welch one-way ANOVA, which does not assume equal variances across groups.
p.adjust.method = "fdr"applies False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction to adjust p-values for multiple pairwise comparisons.
Welch ANOVA result \(p\) = 3.35e-7. This indicates a statistically significant difference in mean Maths scores among the race groups.
The plot also includes Bayesian summaries: \(log_e(BF_{01})\) = −11.63, indicating extremely strong evidence against the null hypothesis
Bayesian \(R^2\) 0.09 means about 9% of variance is explained
Summary: Chinese students show higher mean Maths scores (around 76), while Malay students have lowest means (around57). Both the overall Bayesian test and the pairwise comparisons indicate statistically significant differences in average Maths scores.




3.3.1 ggbetweenstats - Summary of tests


3.4 Significant Test of Correlation: ggscatterstats()
In the code chunk below, ggscatterstats() is used to create a visualisation for a significance test of correlation between Maths and English scores, which assesses whether the observed relationship between the two variables is statistically different from zero.

SHOWggscatterstats(exam, x= MATHS, y=ENGLISH, marginal = TRUE) +
  ggthemes::theme_solarized()













Tip




If marginal = TRUE, marginal histograms or density plots would be added to show the individual distributions of each variable.
Summary: The Pearson correlation coefficient is 0.83 with a p-value of (\(1.70e-83\)), and the Bayesian result shows strong evidence against hull hypothesis \(log_e(BF_{01})\) = -183.55. Both results confirm that Maths and English scores are very strongly and positively correlated.




3.5 Significant Test of Association (Depedence) : ggbarstats() methods
A significant test of association (or dependence) examines whether two categorical variables are related, rather than independent of each other.
The test evaluates:

\(H_0\) (null hypothesis): the two variables are independent (no association)
\(H_1\) (alternative hypothesis): the two variables are associated (dependent)

ggbarstats() creates a bar chart for two categorical variables and automatically performs a statistical test of association, typically a chi-square test of independence (or Fisher’s exact test when appropriate).
First, the Maths scores is binned into a 4-class variable by using cut(). cut() divides the range of a numeric variable into intervals and assigns each value to the interval it falls into. The leftmost interval is coded as the first level, the next as the second level, and so on.

SHOWexam1 <- exam%>%
  mutate(MATHS_bins = (cut(MATHS, breaks = c(0, 60,75,85, 100))))


Thenggbarstats() is used to build a visual for Significant Test of Association

ggbarstats(exam1, x= MATHS_bins, y = GENDER) +
  ggthemes::theme_excel()













Tip




Chi-square test of independence: \(p\) value (0.79) indicates no statistically significant association between gender and Maths score.
\(log_e(BF_{01})\) = 4.73, indicating extremely strong evidence in favour of the null hypothesis (independence).
Summary: the chart shows that Maths score categories are independent of gender with both visual patterns and statistical evidence supporting the conclusion of no association.

text:
A funnel plot is a specialised data visualisation used to support fair and unbiased comparisons across outlets, stores, or business entities. In this hands on exercise, we learn how to create funnel plots using the funnelPlotR package, build static funnel plots with ggplot2, and develop interactive funnel plots by combining ggplot2 with plotly.
Assumption:
All hypothesis tests in this exercise are conducted at the 5% significance level, where the null hypothesis states that no significant difference or no relationship exists between the variables of interest.

text:
3 FunnelPlotR methods
The funnelPlotR package uses ggplot2 to create funnel plots and requires a numerator (events of interest), a denominator (population at risk), and a group variable.






TipKey arguments




limit (95 or 99 plot limits),
label_outliers (to label outlying points),
Poisson_limits and OD_adjust (to add Poisson or overdispersed limits),
xrange and yrange (to control the displayed axis ranges).
Other visual elements such as title and label can also be customised.



The code below uses funnel_plot() to generate a funnel plot the ratio of positive cases to deaths across sub-districts, adjusted for overdispersion. But the y-values are closely clustered and difficult to distinguish visually, so additional customisation is required to improve readability.

funnel_plot(.data = covid19,
            numerator = Positive,
            denominator = Death,
            group = "Sub-district")







A funnel plot object with 267 points of which 0 are outliers. 
Plot is adjusted for overdispersion. 








TipThings to learn from the code chunk above:




In funnel_plot(), group defines the aggregation level of the points rather than a grouping aesthetic as in a scatterplot.
The group argument can be set to sub-district, district, or city, which determines how many points are plotted.
If City is selected, only six data points are shown in the funnel plot.
By default, the data_type argument is set to "SR".
The limit argument controls the funnel limits, where 95 and 99 correspond to the 95% and 99.8% control limits, respectively.




3.1 FunnelPlotR methods: Makeover 1
Here we set adjust x-axis and y-axis range to display more details.

funnel_plot(
  .data = covid19,
  numerator = Death,
  denominator = Positive,
  group = `Sub-district`,
  data_type = "PR",     #<< specifies that the plot uses a proportion or rate
  x_range = c(0, 6500),  #<< sets the x-axis range to focus on sub-districts
  y_range = c(0, 0.05),   #<< sets the y-axis range to display rate 
  theme = funnel_clean())







A funnel plot object with 267 points of which 7 are outliers. 
Plot is adjusted for overdispersion. 








TipThings to learn from the code chunk above:




The data_type argument is used to change the default setting from "SR"(observed/expected, centered around 1) to "PR"(observed A/observed B), so the funnel plot displays proportions instead of standardised ratios,that means changing from relative performance to absolute proportion.
The xrange and yrange arguments are used to control the displayed ranges of the x-axis and y-axis, improving readability when values are tightly clustered.




3.2 FunnelPlotR methods: Makeover 2
Here we add chart title, axis labels and disable the labels for sub-district.

SHOWfunnel_plot(
  .data = covid19,
  numerator = Death,
  denominator = Positive,
  group = `Sub-district`,
  data_type = "PR",   
  x_range = c(0, 6500),  
  y_range = c(0, 0.05),
  label = NA,
  title = "Cumulative COVID-19 Fatality Rate by 
  \nCumulative Total Number of COVID-19 Positive Cases", #<< sets the main title     
  x_label = "Cumulative COVID-19 Positive Cases", #<< customises the x-axis label
  y_label = "Cumulative Fatality Rate"  #<<customises the y-axis label
)







A funnel plot object with 267 points of which 7 are outliers. 
Plot is adjusted for overdispersion. 








TipThings to learn from the code chunk above




label = NA turns off point labelling in the funnel plot to improve visual clarity.
Backticks are used to reference column names that contain nonstandard characters, such as hyphens (Sub-district), spaces, start with numbers etc which would otherwise be interpreted as operators in R.
Althoughfunnel_plot() returns a ggplot object, it is not designed for plotly conversion, and interactive behaviour is limited or unreliable when using ggplotly().

4 Funnel Plot for Fair Visual Comparison: ggplot2 methods
In this section, we learn hands on experience in building funnel plots step by step using ggplot2. The objective is to strengthen the proficiency with ggplot2 for customising specialised data visualisations such as funnel plots.

4.1 Computing the basic derived fields
First, we manually derive the cumulative death rate and the standard error of the cumulative death rate. The formulas are as followed.
\[
\hat{p} = \frac{\text{Deaths}}{\text{Positive}}
\] \[
SE(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}
\]

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death/Positive)%>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate*(1-rate))/(Positive)))%>%
  filter(rate >0) #filter out the record where rate ==0

Next, we useweighted.mean(x, wt) function from base R to calculate the weighted mean. Weighted mean is based on inverse-variance weights so that more precise rate estimates contribute more strongly to the pooled reference value.
\[
\hat{r}_{\text{weighted}}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i r_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i}
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{r_i}{SE_i^2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{SE_i^2}}
\]

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1 / df$rate.se^2)

The weighted mean = 0.0150 is a single pooled reference value used as the centre of the funnel plot.

fit.mean

[1] 0.01496959








Tip




df$rate are the observed death rates for each sub-district
df$rate.se are their standard errors
The weights 1 / df$rate.se^2 are inverse variances
Observations with smaller uncertainty (smaller SE) get more weight




4.2 Calculate lower and upper limits for 95% and 99.9% CI
We use seq(from, to, by, ...) to generate regular sequences of numbers from 1 to 6231, as denominator.

max(df$Positive)

[1] 6231



summary(seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1))

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
      1    1558    3116    3116    4674    6231 


The code chunk below is used to compute the lower and upper limits for 95% and 95% confidence interval and save the results into a table.

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95, number.ll999, 
                   number.ul999, number.seq, fit.mean)

    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center")

4.3 Plotting a static funnel plot
In the code chunk below, ggplot2 functions are used to plot a static funnel plot.


Plot
Code














p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(text = paste(
        "Positive:", Positive,
        "\nRate:", round(rate, 4),
        "\nSub-district:", `Sub-district`)),
    alpha = 0.8, colour = "#1877F2", size = 0.8)+
  
    # OR geom_point(aes(label=`Sub-district`),  alpha=0.4) +

  # ggrepel doesnt work properly with plotly
  #ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = `Sub-district`), max.overlaps = 2, size = 3)+
  
  #reference CI
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll95, linetype ="95% CI"),
            size = 0.4, colour="purple") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul95, linetype ="95% CI"),
            size = 0.4, colour="purple") +
    geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll999, linetype ="99% CI"),
            size = 0.6, colour="darkgreen", alpha = 0.4) + 
      geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul999,linetype ="99% CI"),
            size = 0.6, colour="darkgreen", alpha = 0.4) +
  # weighted mean in the center
   geom_hline(data = dfCI, 
             aes(yintercept = fit.mean, linetype = "Mean"), 
             size = 0.5, 
             colour = "grey40") +
  # up until now the plot is focused around 0, zoom in
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,0.05)) + 
  scale_linetype_manual(
    name = "Reference",
    values = c("95% CI" = "longdash", "99% CI" = "solid", "Mean" = "dashed")) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.13, label = "95%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = -0.18, label = "99%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  ggtitle("Cumulative Fatality Rate by Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +
  xlab("Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") + 
  ylab("Cumulative Fatality Rate") +
  theme_light() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size=12), # control title text size
        legend.position = c(0.91,0.85),     # place legend inside plot area
        legend.title = element_text(size=7),  # reduce legend title size
        legend.text = element_text(size=7),   # reduce legend text size
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey60", linetype = "dotted"),  # legend box
        legend.key.height = unit(0.3, "cm"))   # reduce legend spacing
p










TipLine-type




0 (“blank”): No line.
1 (“solid”):the default
2 (“dashed”): A line made of short, equal-length segments with gaps.
3 (“dotted”): A line composed of dots.
4 (“dotdash”): A pattern of a dot followed by a dash.
5 (“longdash”): A line made of longer dashes.
6 (“twodash”): A pattern of two short dashes followed by a gap.
Legends only appear when we map aesthetics (colour, shape, linetype, etc.) to variables within aes().




4.4 Interactive Funnel Plot: plotly + ggplot2
The interactive funnel plot could be created by using ggplotly() of plotly package.

fp_ggplotly <- ggplotly(p,tooltip = "text")
# OR  tooltip = c("label", "x", "y"))
fp_ggplotly











Caution




text is an aesthetic that belongs to plotly, so it is ignored when the plot is first rendered using static ggplot2.
ggrepel does not work reliably with plotly.









Note




Early in an outbreak or in a small populations, fatality rates look wide. As more case accumulated, fatality rats settled down and converaged toward a stable average.
The CI bands were wide at low cumulative case counts due to high sampling uncertainty and progressively narrowed as case number increase. This implies more stable fatality rate estimates.

title: 05-2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
A correlation coefficient measures the direction and strength of the linear relationship between two variables, with values ranging from −1 to 1. A value of 1 indicates a perfect positive relationship, −1 a perfect negative relationship, and 0 no linear relationship.
For multivariate data, pairwise correlations are typically summarised in a correlation matrix or shown using a scatterplot matrix.
Correlation matrices are used to (1) explore relationships among variables, (2) to support other analyses such as factor analysis and regression, and (3) as a diagnostic tool for detecting issues like multicollinearity.
For large datasets, corrgrams provide a compact visual summary by encoding the sign and magnitude of correlations and reordering variables so that similar ones appear together.
In this hands on exercise, we learn to visualise correlation matrices in R using pairs(), corrplot package, and an interactive Plotly approach.

title: 05-2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
4 Building Correlation Matrix: pairs() method
There are several ways to create a scatterplot matrix in R. In this section, we use the pairs() function from base R graphics. pairs() creates a scatterplot matrix for exploring pairwise relationships among variables. Before proceeding, here is a quick review of the syntax of the pairs() function.

Basic usage: pairs(x) where x is a numeric data frame or matrix.
Formula interface: pairs(~ x + y + z, data = df) uses variables specified in a formula, taken from a data frame.


4.1 Key arugments

labels sets variable names shown on the plot
panel controls how each scatterplot panel is drawn
lower.panel and upper.panel allow different displays below and above the diagonal
diag.panel defines what appears on the diagonal, such as histograms
text.panel controls text on the diagonal
pch, col, cex adjust point style and size
main adds a title
log applies logarithmic scales
subset selects observations
na.action controls handling of missing values

4.2 Building a basic correlation matrix
Figure below shows the scatter plot matrix of Wine Quality Data without the quality and type. It is a 11 by 11 matrix.

pairs(wine[,1:11])







The pairs() function accepts a matrix or data frame as input. In this example, the default pairs() function is used to create a scatterplot matrix from columns 2 to 12 of the wine data frame, which include variables such as acidity, sugar, sulphur dioxide, density, pH, sulphates, and alcohol.

pairs(wine[,2:12])








4.3 Drawing the lower corner
The pairs() function offers many customisation options. Since a correlation matrix is symmetric, it is common to display only one half. To show only the lower half of the scatterplot matrix, the upper.panel argument can be set to NULL.

pairs(wine[,2:12], upper.panel = NULL)







Similarly, we can display the upper half of the correlation matrix by using lower.panel = NULL.

pairs(wine[,2:12], lower.panel = NULL)








4.4 Including with correlation coefficients
Instead of scatterplots, the panel.cor function can be used to display correlation coefficients for each variable pair, with stronger correlations shown in larger text. The syntax is panel.cor(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "", cex.cor). First we can simply run the code and explore the correlation matrix.

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "", cex.cor,...){
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0 ,1))
  r <- abs(cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs"))
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits = digits)[1]
  txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")
  if(missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8/strwidth(txt)
  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) /2)
}

pairs(wine[,2:12], upper.panel = panel.cor)

title: 05-2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
5 Visualising Correlation Matrix: ggcormat()
Correlation matrices become cluttered when datasets are large, making scatterplots hard to interpret. Corrgrams were introduced by D. J. Murdoch and E. D. Chow (1996) and Friendly, M (2002) to address this by visually summarising correlation strength and direction. Several R packages support corrgrams, including corrgram, ellipse, corrplot, and ggstatsplot. In this section, you will learn to visualise a correlation matrix using ggcorrmat() from the ggstatsplot package.

5.1 The basic plot
One advantage of using ggcorrmat() is its ability to produce a comprehensive yet professional statistical summary alongside the correlation matrix.

ggcorrmat(
  data = wine, 
  cor.vars = 1:11)







Next we add more customisations.

ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  # pass additional arguments to the underlying correlation plot
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black", #black border around the cell
                         hc.order = TRUE,  # reorder variables using hierarchical clustering
                         tl.cex = 10), #size of the variable labels
  title = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
  subtitle = "Four Pairs are no significant at p < 0.05"
)








5.1.1 Things to learn from the code chunk above:

The cor.vars argument specifies which variables are used to compute the correlation matrix
while ggcorrplot.args passes additional aesthetic options to ggcorrplot(). Certain arguments should be avoided in this list because they are handled internally, including corr, method, p.mat, sig.level, ggtheme, colors, lab, pch, legend.title, and digits.
The sample sub-code chunk can be used to control specific component of the plot such as the font size of the x-axis, y-axis, and the statistical report.

ggplot.component = list(
    theme(text=element_text(size=5),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8)))


ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  ggcorrplot.args = list(
    outline.color = "black",
    hc.order = TRUE,
    tl.cex = 10
  ),
  title = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
  subtitle = "Four pairs are not significant at p < 0.05",
  ggplot.component = list(
    theme(
      text = element_text(size = 8), #all texts
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10)))
  )

title: 05-2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
6 Building Multiple Plots
Since ggstatsplot is built on ggplot2, it supports faceting. However, faceting is not available in ggcorrmat() itself and must be done using grouped_ggcorrmat() from the ggstatsplot package. .

grouped_ggcorrmat(
  data = wine,
  cor.vars = 1:11,
  grouping.var = type,
  type = "robust",
  p.adjust.method = "holm", #adjust p-values using Holm correction
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 2), #arrange faceted plots in 2 columns
  ggcorrplot.args = list(outline.color = "black",
                         hc.order = TRUE, # reorder variables via hierarchical clustering
                         tl.cex = 10),
  annotation.args = list(
    tag_levels = "a", # add panel tags (a, b, c, ...)
    title = "Correlogram for wine dataset",
    subtitle = "The measures are: alcohol, sulphates, fixed acidity, citric acid, chlorides, residual sugar, density, free sulfur dioxide and volatile acidity",
    caption = "Dataset: UCI Machine Learning Repository"
  )
)








6.1 Key arguments

Faceted correlograms are created by specifying the grouping.var argument.
grouped_ggcorrmat() uses the patchwork package internally to arrange multiple plots. The plotgrid.args argument passes layout options to patchwork::wrap_plots, except for guides, which is handled separately.
The annotation.args argument controls plot level annotations provided by patchwork.

title: 05-2 Visual Correlation Analysis
text:
7 Visualising Correlation Matrix: corrplot Package
In this hands on exercise, the focus is on corrplot, though you are encouraged to explore the other packages as well. An Introduction to corrplot provides a basic understanding of the package.
Here is a summary of the corrplot:

The corrplot package provides a flexible way to visualise a correlation matrix using corrplot(corr, ...), where corr is a correlation matrix computed by cor().
It supports multiple visualisation methods via the method argument, such as method = "circle", "square", "ellipse", "number", "shade", "color", and "pie".
The appearance of the plot can be customised using arguments like col (colour palette), tl.col and tl.cex (text label colour and size), cl.cex (legend size), addgrid.col (grid colour), and mar (margins).
Variables can be reordered using the order argument, for example order = "hclust", "FPC", "AOE", or "alphabet", with hclust.method controlling the clustering method.
The companion function corrplot.mixed() allows different display styles above and below the diagonal using upper = and lower = arguments, such as upper = "ellipse" and lower = "number".


7.1 Getting started with corrplot
Before using corrplot() to draw a corrgram, the correlation matrix must first be computed.The cor() function from base R is used to calculate the correlation matrix for the wine data frame.

wine.cor <- cor(wine[, 1:11])
corrplot(wine.cor)







By default, corrplot() uses circles to display the corrgram and arranges the correlations in a symmetric matrix. A diverging blue–red colour scheme is applied, where blue indicates positive correlations and red indicates negative correlations. Colour intensity AKA saturation represents the strength of the relationship, with darker shades showing stronger correlations and lighter shades indicating weaker ones.

7.2 Working with visual geometrics
The corrplot package provides seven visual geometries, controlled by the method parameter, to encode correlation values: circle, square, ellipse, number, shade, color, and pie. The default method is circle, but this can be changed by specifying the method argument, as shown in the code below.

methods <- c( "square", "ellipse", "number", "shade", "color", "pie")

par(mfrow = c(3,2)) #3*2

for (m in methods){
  corrplot(
    wine.cor,
    method = m,
    title = m,
    mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1) #margin
  )
}








7.3 Working with layout
We experiment with layout options, such as type (full), tl.pos, tl.cex (1), tl.offset (0.4),cl.pos, cl.cex(0.8), and cl.offset (0.5), to further customise the appearance of the corrgram.


type
tl.pos
tl.cex
tl.offset
cl.pos
cl.cex
cl.offset



corrplot() supports three layout types: “full”, “upper”, and “lower”. The default is “full”, which displays the complete correlation matrix. This can be changed using the type argument in corrplot().The default corrgram layout can be further customised. For example, the diag argument can be used to hide the diagonal cells if diag = FALSE, while tl.col changes the axis text label colour to black, as shown in the code and figure below.

types <- c("upper", "lower")
par(mfrow = c(1,2))
for (t in types) {
  corrplot(wine.cor, method = "ellipse", type = t, title = t, diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
}







We also experiment with other layout options, such as tl.pos, tl.cex, tl.offset,cl.pos, cl.cex, and cl.offset, to further customise the appearance of the corrgram.


tl.pos controls position of variable labels: “lt” (left top), “ld”(lower diagonal), “td” (top diagonal), “n” (no labels)

positions <- c("lt", "ld", "td", "n")
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for(p in positions) {
  type_use <- if (p =="td") "upper" else "lower"
  corrplot(wine.cor,
           method = "ellipse",
           diag = FALSE,          
           type = type_use,       
           tl.pos = p,            
           tl.col = "black",      
           mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1)    
  )
  title(paste("tl.pos = '", p, "'", sep = "")) 
}









cex is short for character expansion.
tl.cex controls the size of the variable (text) labels in corrplot().
It is a scaling factor for text size.

tl.cex = 1 default label size
0< tl.cex < 1 smaller labels

-tl.cex > 1 larger labels

cex <- c(0.5, 1, 2) #must be positive
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

for(c in cex) {
  corrplot(wine.cor,
           method = "ellipse",
           diag = FALSE,          
           type = "lower",       
           tl.pos = "ld",            
           tl.col = "black",
           tl.cex = c,
           mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1)    
  )
  title(paste("tl.cex = ", c)) 
}









tl.offset controls how far the variable labels are placed from the corrplot matrix.

Values greater than 1: move the labels further away from the plot.
Values less than 1: move the labels closer to the plot.
A value around 0.4: keeps the default spacing.


offset <- c(-1, 0.4, 1, 2)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for(o in offset) {
  corrplot(wine.cor,
           method = "ellipse",
           diag = FALSE,          
           type = "lower",       
           tl.pos = "ld",            
           tl.col = "black",
           tl.cex = 1,
           tl.offset = o,
           mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1)    
  )
  title(paste("tl.offest = ", o)) 
}









cl.pos controls the position of colour bar.

positions <- c("r", "b", "n")
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

for (p in positions) {
  corrplot(
    wine.cor,
    method = "ellipse",
    type = "lower",
    diag = FALSE,
    tl.col = "black",
    tl.cex = 1,
    tl.offset = 0.4,
    cl.pos = p,
    mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1)
  )
  title(paste("cl.pos =", p))
}









cl.cex controls the font size of the numerical labels on the scale bar.

cl.cex = 0.8 default label size
0< cl.cex < 0.8 smaller labels

-cl.cex > 0.8 larger labels

cex <- c(0.2, 0.8, 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

for (c in cex) {
  corrplot(
    wine.cor,
    method = "ellipse",
    type = "lower",
    diag = FALSE,
    tl.col = "black",
    tl.cex = 1,
    tl.offset = 0.4,
    cl.pos = "r",
    cl.cex = c,
    mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1)
  )
  title(paste("cl.cex =", c))
}









cl.offset controls the position of the numerical labels on the scale bar.

Values greater than -1: move the labels further away from the plot.
Values less than 1: move the labels closer to the plot.
A value around 0.5: keeps the default spacing.


offset <- c(-1, 0.5, 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

for (o in offset) {
  corrplot(
    wine.cor,
    method = "ellipse",
    type = "lower",
    diag = FALSE,
    tl.col = "black",
    tl.cex = 1,
    tl.offset = 0.4,
    cl.pos = "b",
    cl.cex = 0.8,
    cl.offset = o

  )
  title(paste("cl.cex =", o))
}











7.4 Combining Corrgram with the Significant Test
In statistical analysis, it is also important to identify which pairs of variables have statistically significant correlations. The figure below shows a corrgram combined with significance testing, revealing that not all correlation pairs are significant. For example, the correlation between total sulphur dioxide and free sulphur dioxide is statistically significant at the 0.1 level, whereas the correlation between total sulphur dioxide and citric acid is not.
We use the cor.mtest() function from corrplot package to compute p values and confidence intervals for each pairwise correlation.
Here, a 95% confidence level is used. If the p value is less than 0.05, there is statistically significant evidence to reject the null hypothesis that there is no pairwise correlation between the variables.

wine.sig = cor.mtest(wine.cor, conf.level= .95)

Here we can obtain the significance and confidence interval for the correlation between fixed acidity and alcohol.If the confidence interval does not include 0, the correlation is statistically significant at the chosen confidence level.
The correlation between fixed acidity and alcohol is not statistically significant. There is no evidence of a linear relationship between these two variables based on the data.

wine.sig$p["fixed acidity", "alcohol"]

[1] 0.5486749

wine.sig$lowCI["fixed acidity", "alcohol"]

[1] -0.7159033

wine.sig$uppCI["fixed acidity", "alcohol"]

[1] 0.4516043


The resulting p value matrix can be easily visualised by passing it to the corrplot() function using the p.mat argument, as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "number",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45,    #tl
         p.mat = wine.sig$p,
         sig.level = .05)








7.5 Reorder a corrgram
Matrix reordering is important for revealing hidden structures and patterns in a corrgram. By default, variables are shown in their original order, but this can be changed using the order argument in corrplot(). Supported methods include AOE (angular order of eigenvectors), FPC (first principal component), hclust (hierarchical clustering, with various linkage methods), and alphabet. Additional ordering algorithms are available via the seriation package.

AOE


Here, we use corrplot.mixed() with ellipses in the lower triangle and numbers in the upper triangle to improve readability.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               order="AOE",
               tl.col = "black")








7.6 Reordering a correlation matrix using hclust
If using hclust, corrplot() can draw rectangles around the corrgram based on the results of hierarchical clustering. addrect = 3 draws rectangles around three clusters in the reordered matrix to highlight groups of strongly related variables.

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         tl.pos = "lt",
         tl.col = "black",
         order="hclust",
         hclust.method = "ward.D",
         addrect = 3)








corrplot.mixed(
  wine.cor,
  lower = "ellipse",
  upper = "number",
  tl.pos = "lt",
  order = "hclust",
  hclust.method = "ward.D",
  tl.col = "black" # addrect does not work with corrplot.mixed()
)








7.7 alphabet

corrplot.mixed(
  wine.cor,
  lower = "ellipse",
  upper = "number",
  tl.pos = "lt",
  order = "alphabet",
  tl.col = "black"
)








7.8 FPC order

corrplot.mixed(
  wine.cor,
  lower = "ellipse",
  upper = "number",
  tl.pos = "lt",
  order = "FPC",
  tl.col = "black"
)












corrplot.mixed(
  wine.cor,
  lower = "ellipse",
  upper = "number",
  tl.pos = "lt",
  p.mat = wine.sig$p,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  tl.col = "black",
  mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1)
)
title("Correlation matrix with significance (p < 0.05)")













Caution




Different correlation plots may show different significance results because they use different p value adjustments.
corrplot() + cor.mtest() uses raw pairwise correlation tests (no multiple testing correction unless we add it manually).
ggcorrmat() from ggstatsplot applies multiple testing correction (Holm adjustment) by default (or as specified).
corrplot.mixed() and corrplot() do not support grouping or faceting. To show statistical significance by wine type, we must split the data by type, compute the correlation matrix and p values separately for each group, and then draw one corrplot per type with its own title. If we want grouped or faceted correlation plots in a single figure, grouped_ggcorrmat() from ggstatsplot is the more suitable tool.

title: 05-4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
Parallel coordinates plots are designed for visualising and analysing multivariate numerical data. They allow multiple variables to be compared at once and help reveal relationships, such as factors contributing to a Happiness Index. The technique was introduced by Alfred Inselberg in the 1970s and is more common in academic and scientific settings than business reporting. As Stephen Few (2006) notes, parallel coordinates are most effective as an interactive exploration tool for uncovering multivariate patterns.
We will learn how to create static parallel coordinates plots using ggparcoord() from GGally, and interactive parallel coordinates plots using the parallelPlot package.

title: 05-4 Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
4 Plotting Static Parallel Coordinates Plot
ggparcoord() from GGally package is used to create static arallel coordinates plot.

4.1 Key Arguments

data: the data.frame to plot.
columns : which variables (names or indices) become the parallel axes.
groupColumn : a variable (e.g. region) to colour (group) the lines by.
scale : how to scale variables (e.g., "std", "uniminmax"(min 0, max 1), "globalminmax", "robust").
scaleSummary : summary statistic used when centring (scale = "center").
centerObsID : observation to centre on when scale = "centerObs".
missing : how to handle missing values ("exclude", "random", etc.).
order : how to order the axes (can be a custom order or methods like "anyClass").
showPoints : if TRUE, adds points at each variable value.
splineFactor : whether to smooth lines using splines.
alphaLines : transparency (or a column name for per-line alpha) for the lines ( 0 -1).
boxplot / shadeBox : show boxplots or shaded ranges under each axis (TRUE or FALSE).
mapping : additional ggplot2::aes() mappings passed to the plot.
title : plot title.


Plotting a simple parallel coordinates plot
Plotting a parallel coordinates with boxplot
Parallel coordinates with facet
Rotating x-axis text label
Adjusting the rotated x-axis text label



The code below creates a basic static parrallel coordinators plot based on columns 7 to 12.

ggparcoord(data = wh, columns = c(7:12))









The basic parallel coordinates plot did not provide a meaningful interpretation of the World Happiness indicators. Next we improve the plot but adding a range of arguments available in ggparcoord().

wh$Region <- as.factor(wh$Region)


ggparcoord(data = wh, columns = c(7:12),
           groupColumn = "Region",  # Use the column name instead of index
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happiness Variables")









Since ggparcoord() extends ggplot2, we can combine it with ggplot2 functions when creating parallel coordinates plots.
In the code chunk below, facet_wrap() is used to produce 10 small-multiple parallel coordinates plots, with each panel representing one geographical region (for example, East Asia). One aesthetic issue with the current design is that some variable names overlap on the x-axis.

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happines Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region)









we use theme() function from ggplot2 to retate the axis text labels by 30 degrees to make it easy to read.

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happines Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region)+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, vjust = 0.8, size = 5))








4.1.1 Note

To rotate the x-axis text labels, use the axis.text.x argument in the theme() function, and specify element_text(angle = 30) to rotate the x-axis labels by 30 degrees. we can also contronl the y-axis using axis.text.y.
hjust(left 0, centre 0.5, right 1) and vjust(bottom 0, centre 0.5, top 1) control text alignment relative to its position, and they are especially useful after rotating axis labels.
We can also control the axis text size using axis.text.x and axis.text.y in theme().



Rotating the x-axis text labels to 30 degrees causes them to overlap with the plot area. This can be avoided by adjusting the text position using the hjust argument in element_text() within the theme() function. Since we are modifying the appearance of the x-axis labels, we use axis.text.x.

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happines Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region)+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1, size = 5))

section: 5 Plotting Interactive Parallel Coordinates Plot: parallelPlot Methods
text:
5 Plotting Interactive Parallel Coordinates Plot: parallelPlot Methods
parallelPlot is an R package designed specifically for creating parallel coordinates plots using the htmlwidgets framework and d3.js. In this section, we learn how to use the functions in parallelPlot to build interactive parallel coordinates plots.

5.1 Key Arguments of parallelplot()
Here is the refined version with arguments and options wrapped in backticks, using colons, and no references.
Key arguments of parallelPlot():

data: a data frame containing the variables to be visualised
categorical: a named list specifying which columns are categorical and their corresponding levels
refColumnDim: the column name used to colour the lines, which can be continuous or categorical
continuousCS: the colour scale applied when refColumnDim is continuous
categoricalCS: the colour scale applied when refColumnDim is categorical
categoriesRep: controls how categorical variables are displayed, such as EquallySizedBoxes or EquallySpacedLines
arrangeMethod: determines how lines are arranged within categories to minimise crossings, for example fromLeft, fromRight, fromBoth, or fromNone
inputColumns: specifies which columns are treated as input dimensions in the plot
histoVisibility: controls whether histograms are displayed on each axis
invertedAxes: specifies which axes should be inverted or flipped
cutoffs: defines threshold values for variables to filter or highlight observations
refRowIndex: specifies the row index used as a reference baseline line
rotateTitle: controls whether axis titles are rotated
columnLabels: allows custom axis labels, including HTML formatting
sliderPosition: controls which dimensions are initially visible when there are many axes
controlWidgets: enables interactive control widgets, commonly used with Shiny

-cssRules: allows custom CSS styling of the parallel coordinates plot


width and height: specify the size of the interactive widget in pixels

5.2 The basic plot
The code below shows how to use parallelPlot() to create a simple interactive paprallel coordinates plot.
First we select the required columns.

wh <- wh %>%
  select("Happiness score", c(7:12))

After executing the code, we notice that some of the axis labels overlap with each other.

parallelPlot(wh, width = 320, height = 250)






5.3 Rotate axis label
We enable rotateTitle argument to avoid overlapping axis labels.

parallelPlot(wh, rotateTitle = TRUE)





One useful interactive feature of parallelPlot is that when we click on a variable of interest, for example the Happiness score, the default monotonous blue colour changes to a blue colour scale with varying intensity.

5.4 Changing the colour scheme
Since the data is on a continuous scale, we can change the default blue colour by using the continuousCS argument to assign a specific colour scheme to the chart. If the data is discrete (categorical), we can instead use the categoricalCS argument to apply an appropriate categorical colour scheme.

parallelPlot(wh, rotateTitle = TRUE, continuousCS = "YlOrRd")





If we click on a continuous variable, we observe that the colour scheme changes from the default Viridis to a yellow–orange–red gradient, with the colours scaled by intensity.

5.5 Parallel coordinates plot with histogram
The histoVisibility argument can be used to display histograms along the axis of each variable. parallelPlot() expects histoVisibility to be a vector, not a single logical value. The first line creates a logical vector where every element is TRUE, and its length equals the number of columns in wh.

histoVisiblity <- rep(TRUE, ncol(wh))
parallelPlot(wh, rotateTitle = TRUE,
             histoVisibility = histoVisiblity)






5.6 Enabling reference column dimension and flipped axes
Here we enable the reference dimension as Happiness score adn change the direction of the axis.

parallelPlot(
  wh,
  rotateTitle = TRUE,
  refColumnDim = "Happiness score",
  invertedAxes = c("Freedom", "Corruption"))






5.7 Filtering the data before creating the plot
Here we filter the observations with happiness score between 4 and 7.

wh_filtered <- wh[wh$`Happiness score` >= 4 & wh$`Happiness score` <= 7, ]

parallelPlot(
  wh_filtered,
  rotateTitle = TRUE
)

3 Plotting Calendar Heatmap
In this section, we will learn how to programmatically create a calendar heatmap using the ggplot2 package.
By the end of this section, we will be able to:

Plot a calendar heatmap using ggplot2 functions and extensions
Write your own functions using R
Derive date and time fields using base R and lubridate

Prepare data using tidyr and dplyr



3.1 the Data
For this hands-on exercise, the eventlog.csv file will be used. It contains 199,999 rows of time series records of cyber attacks by country.

3.2 Importing the Data
We use read_csv() from the readr package to import the dataset eventlog.csv into the R environment as a tibble named df. We then preview the dataset using kable().

attacks <- read_csv("data/eventlog.csv")

The dataset contains three columns: two categorical variables, source_country and tz, and one timestamp column stored in dttm format.

timestamp stores date and time values in POSIXct format

source_country records the origin of the attack using ISO 3166 1 alpha 2 country codes

tz records the time zone of the source IP address

3.3 Data Preparation


Step 1. Derive weekday and hour of day fields
Step 2. Derive the attacks tibble data frame



We build a function to derived two new fields wkday and hour before plotting the calender heatmap. the fucntion ymd_hms() is used to convert the timestamp based on timezone in the dataset then we create a table to store the source_courty from raw dataset, and extract weekdays and hours from converted timestamp and hours

make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz){
  real_times <- ymd_hms (ts, tz = tz[1],
                         quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
  }







TipNote




ymd_hms() and hour() are from lubridate package
ymd_hms() converts dates stored as character or numeric vectors into POSIXct objects. While ymd_hms() recognises most non alphanumeric date formats, if there are many missing values or invalid strings, the lower level parser parse_date_time() can be used instead.
hour() extracts the hour component from the data-time object.
weekdays() is base R function, that converts a POSIXt or Date object.
The functions weekdays() and months() return a character vector of names based on the current locale.
quarters() returns a character vector from “Q1” to “Q4”.
julian() returns the number of days (possibly fractional) since the origin.






wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday', 
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday', 
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday', 
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp,
                   .$source_country,
                   .$tz)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(wkday = factor(wkday, levels= wkday_levels),
         hour = factor(hour, levels = 0:123))

The function ymd_hms() converts the timestamp using the time zone provided in the dataset. Then the table is rebuilt that keeps the source_country from the raw data and extracts the weekday and hour from the converted timestamp.
Finally, the predefined weekday order and the natural hour order (0 to 23) are applied to the table so the data is properly arranged for plotting.






TipNote



In addition to extracting the required information into the attacks data frame, mutate() from the dplyr package converts the wkday and hour variables into factors so they appear in the correct order when plotting.

  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks", #controls the colour scale.
                      low = "skyblue",
                      high = "darkblue") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Attacks by weekday and time of the day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(), #removes tick marks
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5), #centres the title
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8), #resize 
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6)) #resize













TipNote




A tibble called grouped is created by aggregating the attacks using the wkday and hour variables. A new variable n is produced using count(), which records the number of attacks in each weekday and hour combination. na.omit() removes rows with missing values.
geom_tile() draws the grid cells at each x and y position, where the colour and size arguments control the tile border colour and line width.
theme_tufte() from the ggthemes package removes unnecessary visual clutter to produce a cleaner chart. We comment out this line to compare it with the default ggplot2 appearance. We see dashed outer border and the grey panel background with gridlines), is part of the default ggplot2 theme called theme_gray(). theme_tufte() removes non-informative ink (chart junk) and keep only what helps interpretation.
Choose the theme based on the plot purpose:
Scatterplots: theme_minimal() or default theme_gray()
Publication figures: theme_classic()
Heatmaps, slopegraphs, and calendar plots: theme_tufte() or theme_void()
coord_equal() ensures a 1:1 aspect ratio so the tiles appear square.
scale_fill_gradient() creates a two colour gradient, mapping lower counts to lighter colours and higher counts to darker colours.



We can then group and count the data by hour and wkday and plot it directly. Since values exist for every combination, no additional preprocessing is required.

Step 2: Preparing the tidy data frame

title: 07: Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data
text:
5 Plotting Slopegraph
In this section, we learn how to create a slopegraph using R.
A slopegraph is a efficient chart that shows ranking, actual values, change direction over time all in one visual.
Before starting, make sure CGPfunctions is installed and loaded in the R environment. Then review the guide on using newggslopegraph(), and read the documentation to understand its arguments and usage.






TipKey Arguments




Main arguments of newggslopegraph()
dataframe: dataset used for plotting
Times:x axis variable (usually time such as year)
Measurement: numeric values to compare (y axis)
Grouping: category that forms each slope line (e.g. country, gender)
Common optional arguments
Data.label: labels shown next to points (default: measurement values)
Title, SubTitle, Caption: add text annotations to the chart
LineColor: set line colours (single colour or by group)
LineThickness: adjust thickness of slope lines
Appearance and behaviour options
ReverseYAxis: reverse the y axis (useful for rankings)
ThemeChoice:visual theme (options: “bw”, “tufte”, “wsj”, “econ”, etc.)
RemoveMissing: remove groups with missing values (default: TRUE)




5.1 Step 1: Data Import
Import the rice data set into R environment by using the code chunk below.

rice <- read_csv("data/rice.csv")

title: 08-2 Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
Proportional symbol maps, also called graduated symbol maps, use symbol size to represent the magnitude of a variable, such as counts of populations. They can be either classed (graduated symbols) or unclassed (proportional symbols), where the symbol area is directly proportional to the data value.
In this exercise, we will use the tmap package in R to create a proportional symbol map showing the number of wins at Singapore Pools outlets.

By the end of this hands on exercise, we will be able to use appropriate R packages to:

Import an aspatial data file into R.
Convert it into an sf point object and assign the correct coordinate reference system.
Create interactive proportional symbol maps.

title: 08-2 Visualising Geospatial Point Data
text:
4 Drawing Proportional Symbol Map
To create an interactive proportional symbol map in R, the view mode of tmap is used. The code chunk below switches tmap to interactive mode.

tmap_mode("view")


4.1 It all started with an interactive point symbol map
The code chunks below are used to create an interactive point symbol map.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
           size = 1,
           col = "black",
           lwd = 1)






4.2 Let’s make it proportional
To draw a proportional symbol map, a numeric variable must be mapped to the size visual attribute. The code chunk below assigns the variable Gp1Gp2Winnings to the size aesthetic.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)







4.3 Let’s give it a different colour
The proportional symbol map can be enhanced by adding a colour visual attribute. In the code chunk below, the OUTLET_TYPE variable is mapped to the colour aesthetic.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE", 
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)








4.4 I have a twin brother :)
An impressive and little known feature of tmap view mode is that it also supports faceted maps. The sync argument in tm_facets() can be used to display multiple maps with synchronised zoom and pan behaviour.

tm_shape(sgpools_sf) + 
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE", 
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) + 
  tm_facets(by= "OUTLET TYPE",
            nrow = 1,
            sync = TRUE)

















tmap_mode("plot")
